Potential output, productivity and labour supply

2.33 In our central forecast, we expect potential output growth to fall from around 1½ per cent this year to about 1 per cent next year, as higher energy prices weigh on productive potential. We also expect lower net migration to slow population and labour supply growth, but to have little impact on GDP or real incomes per person. Chart 2.8 shows that we expect potential output growth to then rise to around 1½ per cent in the medium term as market pricing implies a fall back in energy prices.

Chart 2.8: Potential output growth

Source: OBR

2.34 Relative to March, our central forecast is for the level of potential output to be broadly unchanged in the medium term. A downward revision to net migration is offset by a higher starting level of potential output driven by strong recent GDP outturns, which we judge to be structural; and a higher forecast for business investment which slightly raises capital deepening. In per adult terms, potential output is expected to be slightly higher in the medium term than in March as the net migration revision has no impact.

Labour supply

2.35 Labour supply growth is expected to slow from around ¾ of a per cent in 2026 to around 1/3 of a per cent a year over the medium term, marginally lower than in March. The slowdown over the forecast reflects net migration falling this year and then remaining more in line with the previous decade’s average over the next few years, alongside the impact of the ageing population on average hours and participation.

Adult population

2.36 Our forecast for the adult population is based on historical data from the Labour Force Survey (LFS), births and deaths from the latest ONS National Population Projections (NPPs), and our own forecast for net migration. [footnote 6] Based on these, the size of the adult population is forecast to rise by around 320,000 people a year (around 150,000 via net migration), from 56.8 million in 2026 to 58.4 million in 2031. The adult population in 2030 is now expected to be around 50,000 lower than in our March forecast, as shown in the left panel of Chart 2.9, reflecting the downward revision to our net migration forecast partly offset by higher-than-expected outturn population data.

Net migration

2.37 Data published since we finalised the March forecast suggest that net migration will be lower than we previously assumed. The ONS estimates that net migration fell from 331,000 in 2024 to 171,000 in 2025, while visa data up to June 2026 continue to show declines across most visa types. Reflecting these latest data, and informed by our migration model, we expect net migration to fall to 120,000 in the year to mid-2026 (right panel of Chart 2.9).[footnote 7] The near-term decline reflects visa restrictions introduced since 2023 alongside higher emigration following past high levels of immigration, especially among students. Net migration is then forecast to rise gradually to 230,000 by the year to mid-2031, in line with the ‘principal variant’ of the latest ONS population projections. This rise largely reflects our assumption that the net outflow of British nationals and EU nationals who arrived under the pre-Brexit immigration regime will gradually lessen. We judge our net migration forecast to be a reasonable central assumption based on recent outturn data, our modelling infrastructure, and current government policy.

Chart 2.9: Adult population and net migration

Source: ONS, OBR

2.38 Our net migration forecast is around 70,000 a year lower than in March. This has a small negative impact on the level of GDP and potential output in the medium term – but has no impact on per person incomes. The composition of migration is also important for economic and fiscal outcomes, with the following being important factors:

  • Demographics: on arrival, migrants are generally more likely to be of working age with around 80 per cent of migrants being aged 16-64 – compared to around 60 per cent for the wider UK population – in the principal variant of the ONS 2024-based NPPs.

  • Participation: on arrival, migrants tend to have a lower rate of participation at a given age than the domestic population. This generally offsets the effect of demographics and means that the average migrant tends to have a similar overall participation rate. See Box 2.3 of the March 2024 EFO and Box 2.3 of the November 2023 EFO for more detail on these assumptions.

  • Productivity: we assume migrants have broadly the same average rate of productivity as the domestic population. This judgement is highly uncertain as it depends on a range of factors related to the characteristics of migrants which we explored in more detail in Box 2.1 of the March 2026 EFO.

2.39 We consider all of these factors when assessing the impact on the labour market of revisions to our overall net migration forecast, as the composition of the migrant population will vary significantly across different entry routes.[footnote 8] The downward revision to net migration in this forecast is broad-based across various visa routes so we judge that this revision has no impact on the overall participation rate or level of productivity. This means that we assume that lower net migration will leave GDP per person, an indicator of average living standards, unchanged by the end of the forecast.

2.40 There remains considerable uncertainty around our net migration forecast, including the impact of previous policy changes on the outlook for student visas, the share of humanitarian arrivals from Ukraine that remain in the UK, and the future level of net migration of EU nationals. Potential changes to indefinite leave to remain policy, which are not currently reflected in our forecast as the policy details are not sufficiently certain, and changes to visa salary requirements, the details of which were confirmed after the deadline for inclusion in the economy forecast, may also affect net migration in future. We explored the economic impact of two alternative scenarios of higher and lower medium-term net migration in Box 2.3 of the March 2024 EFO. In these scenarios, we also demonstrated the impacts of using alternative assumptions for migrants’ productivity and participation in the labour force, which are significant.

Participation rate and average hours

2.41 Our forecasts for trend labour force participation and average hours are unchanged from March. The trend labour force participation rate is forecast to fall slightly from 63½ per cent in 2026 to 63¼ per cent in 2030, while trend average hours fall marginally from 32 hours a week in 2026 to 31¾ hours a week in 2030. Both decline because of our assumption that the population will continue to age, and that older people, on average, have lower participation rates and work fewer hours. The decline in average hours is more gradual than had been the case before the financial crisis, as we assume that the weakness in productivity growth since then limits workers’ capacity to use part of their increase in real wages to increase their amount of leisure time. The recent ONS revisions to historical average hours, which were published after we finalised our forecast, suggest that average hours growth has been lower, and output per hour higher, than we had previously thought. We discuss these revisions in detail in Box 2.2.

Productivity

2.42 We assume that trend productivity growth slows in 2027 to 0.7 per cent, largely because of the spike in energy prices.[footnote 9] Productivity growth is then forecast to rise to 1.1 per cent in 2031 as energy prices fall back. We assume the slightly higher medium term fossil fuel prices in financial market pricing do not reduce medium-term productivity, as firms adjust production processes and energy sources (see Box 2.1 for more details).

2.43 The main change to our forecast for trend productivity growth since March is a stronger contribution from capital deepening, largely reflecting a higher path for business investment following consistently stronger-than-expected outturns. This change, combined with slightly higher-than-expected growth in the first half of 2026, leaves the level of trend productivity around 0.2 per cent higher than in the March forecast in 2030. We have not changed our previous judgement that underlying trend total factor productivity growth reaches 0.8 per cent in 2030, which we explained in Briefing paper No.9: Forecasting productivity. The recent ONS revisions to productivity were published after we finalised this forecast, but we discuss them in Box 2.2. We will incorporate the impact of any changes, alongside other developments, in our next forecast.

Alternative measure of productivity

2.44 Labour market data remain a key source of uncertainty for the productivity outlook. Chart 2.10 compares an LFS-based measure of labour productivity with an alternative measure created by the Resolution Foundation, based on HMRC PAYE real time information on employees and administrative data on self-employment. The two measures now suggest similarly weak cumulative growth since the pandemic (shown in the right panel), despite considerably different paths to get there. This demonstrates the uncertainty around even recent trends in productivity growth. We remain cautious about interpreting trends from recent data from relatively short periods and we will continue to regularly review our productivity assumption to consider any new information, such as the component-based data discussed in Box 2.2.

2.45 The development and adoption of AI is widely expected to boost future productivity growth, and we previously analysed this in Annex B of Briefing paper No.9: Forecasting productivity. Sectoral data can help to shed light on the degree to which AI is already enhancing UK productivity growth. Initially, it might be expected that ‘AI-producing’ sectors would experience an acceleration in productivity growth, and then over time this would spread to ‘AI-adopting’ sectors. According to the latest ONS Business Insights and Conditions Survey, only 30 per cent of businesses reported using at least one type of AI technology in September 2026, though this is up from 15 per cent two years ago.

2.46 While sectoral data over short periods can be highly volatile, data on output per worker based on administrative sources suggests recent growth in productivity has been broad-based.[footnote 10] Table 2.2 shows that growth between the final quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026 has accelerated compared to previous periods in some of the sectors most associated with the production and use of AI services, such as IT and communications, and professional, scientific and technical services. But productivity growth was relatively strong in these sectors prior to the pandemic, and growth has also accelerated in sectors likely to be currently less affected by AI, such as accommodation and food, and wholesale and retail. We will continue to closely monitor the emerging evidence and how to reflect it in our forecasts for productivity and employment.

Box 2.2: Recent ONS revisions to historical economic data

In the period since we closed our forecast to new data,a the ONS has released revised historical National Accounts and hourly productivity data.

Blue Book-consistent Quarterly National Accounts figures

The Blue Book is the ONS’s annual update to the sources and methods used in the UK National Accounts, and the Quarterly National Accounts published on 30 September were consistent with the 2026 Blue Book. Real GDP growth between 1997 and the second quarter of 2026 has been revised upward by an annual average of 0.1 percentage points. Growth in 2025 was revised down by 0.1 percentage points, and growth in the first half of 2026 revised up by the same amount. Blue Book revisions only have a small impact on the starting level of nominal GDP in our forecast – which is important as the denominator for fiscal aggregates – raising it by 0.1 per cent in the second quarter of 2026. There were also relatively limited changes to the composition of GDP. Given these modest revisions to the recent momentum in the economy, and to the starting level and composition of nominal GDP, it is unlikely that incorporating the Blue Book 2026 revisions would have had a material impact on our economy or fiscal forecasts.

Average hours and productivity

Productivity growth is one of the most important, but uncertain, judgements for our economy and fiscal forecasts. One of the sources of uncertainty relates to challenges in accurately measuring both the level of, and growth in, historical productivity.

Our preferred measure of productivity is output per hour worked.b To estimate total hours worked, the ONS previously used a ‘direct approach’ which drew on average hours worked reported in the Labour Force Survey. The ONS will now be moving towards a ‘component approach’ to calculate hourly productivity that draws on a wider range of data sources to construct estimates of labour input, in line with the latest international standards.c Revisions have, so far, been published on a whole-economy basis up to 2024. Previous OECD research finds that countries which rely on average hours taken directly from labour force surveys systematically overestimate labour input and so underestimate hourly productivity.d The ONS published this new approach after we had finalised the pre-measures forecast, so we did not reflect it in the forecast, and it will become the official estimate for hourly productivity from November.

Chart D shows that average hours worked are materially lower under this new methodology and have continued their pre-financial crisis downward trend, falling at an average annual rate of 0.3 per cent between 2010 and 2024. The difference between the direct and component approaches is largely explained by reducing the use of imputation when measuring the amount of annual leave taken, leading to higher measured annual leave and lower hours worked.e The revisions to average hours have not changed output or income, but have significantly changed the working hours required to produce that output.

The small change in the contribution to GDP growth from employment reflects revisions to the number of workers from taking on new data sources, which results in a small change in output per worker.

Output gap and real GDP

Output gap

2.47 Our swathe of output gap models, shown in Chart 2.11, points to a widening amount of spare capacity in the economy. The models are based on a variety of methods including statistical filters on GDP, extracting common trends from surveys of capacity utilisation, and structural filters using economic relationships with variables like inflation to make inferences about the output gap. Based on these and other indicators, our central estimate is that GDP is just over 1 per cent below its potential level at the start of the forecast. In the second half of this year, we expect higher energy prices to weigh on aggregate demand to a greater extent than supply, widening the output gap further. Relative to March, higher interest rate expectations also push down on our output gap forecast. As energy prices fall back, as implied by the market pricing that underpins our forecast, we expect a steady cyclical recovery in our central forecast, with the output gap closing by 2031.

Chart 2.11: Output gap

Source: OBR

Real GDP

2.48 Real GDP growth was robust around the start of the Middle East conflict, with quarterly growth of 0.6 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, but we expect higher energy prices to begin to weigh on growth from the second half of 2026. Our central forecast, shown in the left panel of Chart 2.12, is for real GDP growth of around 1¼ per cent in 2026, a slight improvement on our March forecast reflecting significantly higher-than-expected first-quarter growth.[footnote 11] In the second half of 2026 and into 2027, we expect higher global energy prices to feed through to the prices facing consumers and businesses, and higher interest rates to weigh on activity. We have therefore downgraded our central forecast for real GDP growth in 2027 to 1 per cent, 0.5 percentage points below our March forecast. As energy prices are then expected to fall back, our central forecast sees growth pick up to average 1¾ per cent a year over the rest of the forecast period. This leaves the level of GDP in 2030 broadly unchanged from our March forecast.

2.49 We judge that the risks around our central forecast are broadly balanced. The right panel of Chart 2.12 shows that, based on our historical forecast errors, there is a one-in-five chance that real GDP growth in 2027 could be higher than 2¼ per cent and a similar chance that real GDP contracts. In practice, the risks to the forecast will likely be different to those in the past. Upside risks to real GDP growth include a faster reduction in energy prices than we assume and stronger productivity growth, potentially driven by the wider adoption of AI. Downside risks include a larger or more persistent energy shock than implied by market pricing, increased geopolitical uncertainty, more disruption to trade due to uncertainty and the impact of tariffs, and weaker productivity growth. We explore the implications for growth of alternative energy price paths in Chapter 7. There is also a significant risk of wider unexpected shocks hitting the UK economy, with recent examples being the Covid pandemic and Russian invasion of Ukraine. These shocks tend to be larger on the downside than the upside and may result in large differences between forecast and outturn.

Chart 2.12: Real GDP

Source: ONS, OBR

2.50 Real GDP per person, an indicator of living standards, is 0.7 per cent higher in 2030 than in our March forecast. This is mainly explained by a higher starting level of potential output, with a small contribution over the forecast from higher growth in capital deepening. The lower forecast for net migration has very little impact on GDP per person as we judge that those net migrants would have had similar labour market characteristics to those of the general population, explained in paragraph 2.38.

Labour market

2.51 Labour market conditions continue to loosen as vacancies and the number of payrolled employees fall, while private sector pay growth has eased. Given the acknowledged issues with data quality within the LFS, we continue to draw on a wide range of evidence in our assessment of labour market conditions, including administrative data and surveys.[footnote 12] This is particularly the case for the participation rate and, consequently, employment growth. The left panel of Chart 2.13 illustrates that non-LFS measures of employment point to a subdued labour market, in contrast to the continued growth in LFS employment. Survey evidence, such as the latest Bank of England Decision Makers Panel, also points to broadly flat employment growth over the past year. HMRC administrative data suggest this continues to be driven by lower inflows into employment rather than higher outflows from employment. We also expect the Employment Rights Act 2025 (ERA) to weigh on the labour market, in addition to previously announced policies including the increases in employer NICs and the National Living Wage. See Chapter 3 for a detailed discussion of the impact of policy measures on the labour market.

2.52 The general trend in the LFS unemployment rate matches this picture of a loosening labour market, rising from its post-pandemic trough of 3.6 per cent in 2022 to 5.2 per cent in the final quarter of 2025 (right panel of Chart 2.13). While the unemployment rate in the LFS fell to 4.9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, other evidence – such as the number of vacancies, the KPMG and REC UK Report on Jobs, and the employment component of the UK PMI – signal ongoing weakness in labour demand. Given these wider indicators, we expect the unemployment rate to rise marginally from its current level, peaking at just above 5 per cent in the second quarter of 2027, before falling to its estimated equilibrium rate of 4.1 per cent. The peak in unemployment is marginally lower than in our March forecast but comes a year later. We previously explored scenarios with alternative trajectories for the unemployment rate in our March 2026 EFO.

Households

Household saving rate

As described in paragraph 2.30, we are forecasting real household disposable incomes to fall slightly in the near term. In the face of this, we expect consumers to gradually reduce saving to smooth their consumption over time. There are significant risks around this forecast. For example, if higher interest rates or general economic uncertainty encourage higher precautionary saving, consumption would be weaker than in our forecast.

Household consumption

2.54 Real household consumption has stagnated since the pandemic, with its level in 2025 only 1 per cent higher than in 2019. We expect real household consumption growth to average ¾ of a per cent in 2026 and 2027, as weak real income growth weighs on spending growth. It then picks up to grow more in line with overall GDP in the medium term, following the recovery in real income growth. This leaves real consumption as a share of GDP at 61 per cent at the end of the forecast, over 2 percentage points below the average level from 2010-2019, and 0.4 percentage points below the level we forecast in March. The relatively weak growth in consumption reflects higher energy prices (and that these constitute a larger shock to real household disposable incomes than real GDP) and a higher share of consumption occurring via government-provided services since the pandemic.

Business sector

Profits

2.55 The rate of return on corporate capital and the profit share of GDP are both currently at low levels relative to recent history (Chart 2.15). After a period when firms have absorbed a range of cost increases into lower profits, including the rises in employer NICs and energy prices, we increasingly expect them to pass these costs on to households and rebuild their profit margins. Increasing real wages by slightly less than productivity growth should push up the rate of return and profit share towards more historically typical levels. The relatively loose labour market is likely to underpin this process by reducing workers’ bargaining power.

Business investment

2.56 Real business investment rose by around 2½ per cent over the first half of 2026, leaving its level 2 per cent above our March forecast by the second quarter of 2026. We expect some of this recent strength to unwind as headwinds from higher energy prices weigh on business activity and investment over 2027. We then expect growth in business investment to pick up, averaging 1¼ per cent a year. By 2030, we expect the level to be ½ a per cent above our March forecast, reflecting both its recent strength and a higher profits forecast.

Government

2.57 Real government spending, the sum of government consumption and investment, is expected to grow by just under 4 per cent in 2026, up from 2 per cent in 2025. Growth then slows to average 1¼ per cent over the remainder of the forecast. Weaker real departmental spending growth in the medium term leaves the level of total government spending around ½ a per cent lower in 2030 relative to our March forecast. Within government spending, consumption rises from 21 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 21¼ per cent in 2026. It then settles at around 21 per cent of GDP by the end of the forecast, significantly higher than the 19½ per cent in 2019. Government investment follows a similar profile, increasing from just under 3½ per cent of GDP in 2025 to nearly 4 per cent in 2027, before falling back to around 3½ per cent by 2031. This is around ¾ of a percentage point above the level in 2019.

Current account and sectoral balances

2.58 We forecast the current account deficit of the balance of payments to narrow from just over 3 per cent of GDP in 2025 to around 2½ per cent by 2030, as export growth outpaces import growth. Chart 2.16 shows how the matching inflow of foreign saving to fund this deficit represents a steady inflow of net lending from the rest of the world. As weak income growth drives a fall in household saving, we expect the household net lending position to fall from a surplus of around 1¾ per cent of GDP in 2026 to a deficit of 1¼ per cent by 2031. The corporate sector moves from a small deficit to a surplus by 2030 as firms rebuild the rate of return and investment falls slightly as a share of GDP. The public sector deficit narrows significantly over the forecast, but the profile remains similar to our March forecast.

The housing market

Mortgage rates

2.59 We expect that the average effective interest rate on the outstanding stock of mortgages will rise from 4 per cent in 2026 to around 5 per cent in 2031. This is due to an upward-sloping yield curve pushing up quoted rates, and people rolling off mortgages that were fixed when rates were lower. As illustrated in the left panel of Chart 2.17, this effective rate is higher than the average since the financial crisis (3 per cent), but significantly lower than over the decades leading up to 2008. The stock of outstanding mortgage debt is around 85 per cent of household disposable income across the forecast period. This is lower than the peak during the financial crisis, but higher than at any time before the early 2000s, when effective mortgage rates were significantly higher. The right panel of Chart 2.17 shows that mortgage payments as a share of household disposable income are expected to rise to reach 4¼ per cent in 2031, the highest since 2009 and more than double the 2021 level of 2 per cent.

Compared to the March forecast, we expect 190,000 fewer cumulative net additions over the forecast period. 2.61 We have not changed our estimate from the March 2025 forecast that the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF), on its own, would boost housebuilding significantly. But leading indicators, particularly housing permissions, suggest that housing supply will remain substantially weaker than would be consistent with our previous forecasts in the near term (see Chart 2.19). Over the medium term, we judge that the economic environment, including as a result of higher interest rates, and the wider regulatory picture, mean net housing additions are likely to rise more slowly than we previously expected:

  • Higher interest rates since late 2022, alongside other affordability pressures and weak effective demand, have weighed on the commercial viability of residential development. Industry evidence suggests that higher borrowing costs and weaker buyer sentiment have weighed on house price growth, reducing developers’ ability to absorb rising costs.[footnote 13] This points to a flatter near-term profile for net additions, with some medium-term recovery expected as some of these economic conditions improve.

  • The weaker profile for housing supply in the near and medium term also partly reflects the cumulative effect of regulatory and fiscal changes outside the planning system over the last decade, particularly since 2019. These policy developments have increased the cost, complexity, and timescales associated with residential development. These include measures aimed at improving building safety, such as the Building Safety Levy and Building Safety Regulator regime, environmental requirements such as Biodiversity Net Gain and nutrient mitigation schemes, and wider fiscal measures including the residential property developer tax and higher corporation tax rates. Taken together, these measures appear to have weighed on housebuilding activity to a greater extent than we had previously assumed.

House prices and property transactions

2.62 We estimate that average house prices will grow by around 2 per cent in 2026 and by 2½ per cent in 2027. This would continue the recent trend of house price growth being below CPI inflation, largely driven by higher mortgage rates and stagnating real incomes. We then expect house price growth to average 2¾ per cent from 2028 onwards, as real income growth recovers. Compared to the March forecast, growth in house prices is therefore lower in the near term. The outlook for house prices remains highly sensitive to the path of mortgage rates, the evolution in real incomes, and the impact of planning and regulatory changes on housing supply. The ’Your First Home‘ scheme could marginally raise house prices by stimulating housing demand.

2.63 In our central forecast, property transactions grow from around 1.2 million in 2026 to around 1.3 million in 2031, as the housing market turnover rate returns to its assumed medium-term equilibrium that every house is transacted on average once every 24 years and as the housing stock continues to grow. The number of transactions across the forecast period is around 4 per cent lower than in the March forecast, as higher mortgage rates are expected to weigh on activity, and as we have revised down our forecast for growth in the housing stock.

Residential investment

2.64 Real residential investment (excluding transfer costs) is forecast to rise by 0.5 per cent in 2026, following weaker-than-expected outturns in the first half of the year, 0.2 percentage points lower than in our March forecast.[footnote 14] Growth then picks up to average around 3 per cent a year over the rest of the forecast, around 2 percentage points lower than in our March forecast. This leaves real residential investment 6¾ per cent lower in 2030 than in our March forecast. This weaker outlook is due to lower planned housing completions on new-build investment but is partially offset by diverted investment toward improving the existing stock.

Nominal GDP and its composition

2.65 We expect nominal GDP growth to slow from around 4 per cent in 2026-27 to 3¼ per cent in 2027-28, as growth in both real GDP and the GDP deflator slows. We then expect nominal GDP growth to average around 3¾ per cent a year over the rest of the forecast, as real GDP growth rises and inflation sits at around 2 per cent. Compared to the March forecast, cumulative growth in nominal GDP from 2025-26 to 2030-31 is 1¼ percentage points higher. This difference is driven almost entirely by higher growth in the GDP deflator. Whole-economy inflation is higher due to the second-round effects of the imported energy shock through wages and profits, and a rise in the price of energy produced in the UK.

2.66 This is reflected in stronger cumulative growth in all major components of nominal GDP, both in income and expenditure terms. On the income side, we expect strong growth in nominal corporate profits, a determinant of corporation tax receipts, averaging around 4½ per cent a year over the forecast period. Growth in nominal labour income, including wages and salaries and mixed incomes, averages just over 3 per cent a year over the forecast period. Labour income growth is a key judgement in the forecast given its comparatively high effective tax rate and that income tax thresholds are currently frozen. On the expenditure side, we expect nominal business investment growth to average around 2¼ per cent a year across the forecast, while nominal household consumption growth averages 3¾ per cent a year.

Chapter 3: Policy measures

Introduction

3.1 The Charter for Budget Responsibility states that the responsibility for producing the costings of policy measures lies with the responsible policy department, which is typically HM Revenue and Customs for tax policies and the Department for Work and Pensions for welfare policies. These departments therefore hold the models and datasets that are used to produce these costings. The OBR’s role, as set out in the Charter, is to provide independent scrutiny and certification of these costings.[footnote 17] Requests for further information relating to the methodology and datasets used for costings should therefore initially be directed to the relevant department.

Total effect of Government decisions

The impact of fiscal policy decisions on borrowing

3.2 This forecast incorporates the fiscal implications of policy measures announced in this Budget and since the March forecast, which are summarised in Table 3.1 and Chart 3.1. The direct effect of these measures is to increase borrowing by £7.6 billion in 2026-27, £3.5 billion in 2027-28, and £0.4 billion in 2028-29. The direct effect of policy measures reduces borrowing thereafter by £4.1 billion in 2029-30, £5 billion in 2030-31 and £12 billion in 2031-32.

3.3 Policies that affect public spending are estimated to increase borrowing between 2026-27 and 2030-31 by an average of £3.3 billion, before planned spending reductions are estimated to reduce borrowing by £4.2 billion in 2031-32. This reflects:

  • Funding to support a £100 council tax rebate increases spending this year (2026-27) by £2.6 billion.

  • Funding for the defence investment plan is estimated to increase spending by an average of £1.8 billion a year. The valuation of unfunded public sector pensions increases spending by an average of £1.1 billion a year across the forecast.

  • Reductions in planned capital spending of £0.9 billion a year from 2027-28. The civil service transformation programme is estimated to reduce resource spending by £0.5 billion a year from 2028-29. In 2031-32, a reduction in the pre-measures spending assumption further reduces resource spending by £5.5 billion.

3.4 Changes to tax policy increase borrowing by £1.7 billion in 2026-27, before reducing borrowing by an average of £6 billion over the final four years of the forecast. This reflects:

  • The further freeze to fuel duty and the temporary zero-rating of VAT on domestic electricity reduce receipts in 2026-27 by £1.3 billion.

  • HMRC tax administration, compliance and debt collection measures raise an additional £3.6 billion by 2031-32. The largest of these measures is the introduction of timely payment for self assessment which is estimated to yield an average of £1.6 billion a year from 2029-30.

  • Changes to corporation and bank taxes are estimated to raise an average of £2.2 billion a year across the forecast. The reduction in writing down allowances is estimated to raise approximately £1 billion a year on average from 2027-28, while the temporary increase in the bank surcharge increases receipts by £1 billion in 2027-28.

  • Further increases to tax rates on savings and property income increase receipts by an average of £1 billion a year from 2028-29.

Economic effects of policy measures

3.8 Our forecast explicitly accounts for the economic impacts of newly announced government policy where these are material. The impacts of policy on the supply side of the economy are explicitly accounted for in our forecast if credible evidence suggests the measures will have an additional, durable, and significant impact on potential output.[footnote 18] The Government has announced initial details of a range of policies since the March forecast – including at this Budget – which aim to raise GDP over the longer term. We will review the potential impact of such policies, over the medium- and long-term, when final details are confirmed and where sufficient evidence is available – including as part of our annual summer assessments of supply potential. Therefore, in this forecast, we have not made any explicit adjustments to potential output due to policy changes.[footnote 19]

3.9 Our assessment of the demand-side effects of fiscal policy is informed by ‘fiscal multipliers’. We define fiscal multipliers as the impact of a policy package on demand which, at least in the short run, can affect the output gap by changing the level of economic activity relative to potential output. Our standard multipliers are drawn from the empirical literature. However, there is no single multiplier that applies to all policies and at all points in the economic cycle. The multiplier may vary due to macroeconomic conditions and policy instruments. We therefore assess at each forecast what multipliers are appropriate.[footnote 20] We judge that the demand-side impact of this policy package is not sufficiently material to explicitly adjust our real GDP forecast. The overall package is relatively small in fiscal terms and much of the initial fiscal loosening has been pre-announced. Additionally, forward-looking agents may smooth economic activity through the initial fiscal loosening and subsequent fiscal tightening arising from policy.

3.10 The changes to fuel duty and the temporary cut to VAT on domestic electricity bills have small effects on our inflation forecast. They reduce CPI inflation by 0.08 percentage points in 2026-27 and 0.02 percentage points in 2027-28, before raising CPI inflation by 0.04 percentage points in 2028-29. On a quarterly basis, at its peak, these policies reduce CPI inflation by 0.22 percentage points in the second quarter of 2027 and increase CPI inflation by 0.16 percentage points in the second quarter of 2028.[footnote 21],[footnote 22]

Spending measures included in this forecast

Changes to departmental expenditure

3.11 Changes to departmental spending increase borrowing by £5 billion in 2026-27 and £1.2 billion in 2027-28, before reducing borrowing by £6 billion in 2031-32. We discuss changes to departmental spending in greater detail in Chapter 5. The largest changes are:

  • a £100 council tax rebate for properties in bands A to D in England which increases borrowing by £2.6 billion in 2026-27;

  • the defence investment plan, which increases departmental resource spending (RDEL) by £1.8 billion a year on average;

  • a £5.5 billion reduction to the RDEL pre-measures spending assumption in 2031-32; and

  • changes to departmental capital spending, which reduce borrowing by an average of £0.9 billion a year from 2027-28.

Other spending policies

3.12 Other policies contributing to the changes in spending in this forecast include:

  • The valuation of public service pension schemes and consequent reduction in employer contributions, which increases net spending on unfunded pension schemes by an average of £17 billion per year in the medium-term. The Government has decided to reduce departmental resource spending in line with the lower cost of employer contributions, by an average £16 billion from 2027-28 onwards. The overall net effect of these changes is therefore to increase overall spending by an average of £1.1 billion from 2027-28. This net cost arises from the participation of employers in public service pension schemes whose staff costs are not funded through departmental spending, so the lower employer contributions are not offset. This policy is discussed in greater detail in Chapter 5.

  • A package of further measures to address fraud and error in the welfare system is expected to reduce welfare spending by £0.5 billion in 2031-32. This includes the hiring of 2,000 verification assurance officers, 200 additional staff to prevent fraud and error from those living abroad, and 150 additional staff to reduce capital-related fraud and error in pension credit. We discuss the staffing and departmental spending implications of these measures in more detail in paragraphs 3.14 and 3.15.

Receipts measures included in this forecast

Tax administration, compliance, and debt collection measures

3.13 The Government has announced further HMRC tax administration, compliance, and debt collection measures in this Budget which are estimated to raise an additional £3.6 billion by 2031-32. These measures are targeted at the current high levels of tax debt and reducing the overall tax gap through increased HMRC compliance activity, and include:

  • The introduction of timely payment for self assessment, and part reversal of the Budget 2025 measure that mandated coding out via the PAYE system, which brings more payments of self-assessment liabilities forward into the tax year in which income is earned. This measure is estimated to yield an average of £1.6 billion a year from 2029-30 which reflects the timely payment system preventing some debt losses and changing the timing of recovery of debt. The yield is adjusted to account for self-assessment customers reducing their forecast liabilities and additional delayed debt created due to payment pressures in the transition year. Further information on the non-debt cash timing impacts of the measure is detailed in paragraph 3.25.

  • Changes to HMRC’s compliance workforce which are estimated to yield an additional £0.4 billion in 2031-32. This accelerates the recruitment of the previously announced 5,500 additional HMRC compliance officers and funds an additional 670 staff by the end of 2029-30. The recruitment of these compliance officers will be equivalent to a 23 per cent increase to HMRC’s compliance workforce compared to March 2024. The expected yield has been adjusted to account for diminishing returns of additional compliance officers, where marginal yield from additional activity is likely to be below the average yield from business-as-usual compliance activity, disruption impacts, and optimism bias to reflect uncertainty around recruitment, performance of staff, and nature of future non-compliance activity.

  • Other measures which yield £1.4 billion in 2031-32, and include extending HMRC’s powers to directly recover outstanding tax debts; mandating the use of e-invoicing to reduce opportunities for error and other forms of non-compliance; investing to place part of the established stock and future flows of outstanding tax debt with debt collection agencies; and extending the VAT online marketplace liability rules to UK businesses, with a minimum platform threshold at £90,000. The interactions between measures targeted at debt collection have been captured by adjusting the tax bases to capture the reduced revenue available to collect as a result of measures targeting the same customer group or types of debt.

Box 3.1: Compliance policy and the tax gap

In our scrutiny of tax compliance policies, in addition to considering the impact of each measure individually, we also consider the overall impact of the full package of measures on the projected ‘tax gap’. This is the difference between the amount of tax that should, in theory, be paid and the amount received, and so is a measure of overall non-compliance. While most tax liabilities are paid voluntarily through the normal operation of the tax system, other liabilities are only identified or recovered through HMRC compliance activity. HMRC records the additional revenue generated, and losses prevented through this activity as ‘compliance yield’. Other things equal, higher yield from compliance and debt collection activities should reduce the amount of tax that ultimately remains unpaid and, in turn, the tax gap.

HMRC’s latest estimate of the tax gap was £59 billion or 6.4 per cent of total theoretical liabilities in 2024-25 (left-hand side, Chart A).a These estimates suggest the tax gap has risen since the mid-2010s, following a period of decline, although the increase appears to have flattened in recent years.b As shown on the right-hand side of Chart A, small businesses have accounted for a growing share of the tax gap in recent years, rising from around 40 per cent of the total in 2017-18 to more than 60 per cent since 2021-22. Of the compliance measures announced in this Budget, a third of the yield is expected to reduce the tax gap, with the residual reflecting either debt acceleration or payments. Of the 15 measures expected to reduce the tax gap announced this Budget, four target the small business tax gap.

Changes to corporation and bank taxes

3.16 The Budget includes several changes to corporation and bank taxes, which increase receipts by £2.3 billion in 2031-32. These include:

  • A reduction to the writing down allowance (WDA) main rate from 14 to 12 per cent, alongside an increase in the new first-year allowance introduced in January 2026 from 40 to 50 per cent from April 2027.[footnote 23] This is estimated to raise an average of £1 billion per year from 2027-28.

  • A temporary 3 percentage point increase to the bank surcharge, from 3 to 6 per cent, effective from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028. Over the 15 months this is in effect, it is estimated to yield a total of £1.5 billion. This is net of an estimated £190 million reduction in receipts[footnote 24] as some banks are assumed to move profits out of the UK in response to the higher tax rate. The size of this effect is uncertain.

  • Restricting sovereign wealth and overseas public pension funds’ immunity from direct taxes on UK income and gains from January 2029 raises £0.7 billion by 2029-30. This estimated yield includes a behavioural effect which significantly reduces the costing to reflect the affected population restructuring their assets, increasing leverage, and an attrition adjustment. This costing is deemed highly uncertain because of a lack of administrative data on the tax and assets of the affected group, and uncertainty surrounding the degree to which these groups will respond to minimise the impact of these changes.

Increase to tax rates on savings and property income

3.17 This Budget further increases the tax rates on savings and property income. These rates were already set to increase by 2 percentage points in April 2027 following measures announced at Budget 2025. From April 2027, the basic, higher, and additional rates will increase by a further 2 percentage points to 24, 44, and 49 per cent respectively. Together, the measures announced at this Budget are estimated to raise £1.0 billion by 2031-32:

  • The additional 2 percentage point increase in all rates of saving income tax is estimated to yield £0.6 billion a year on average from 2028-29. A behavioural response, primarily reflecting additional usage of other tax advantaged assets, such as Individual Savings Accounts, reduces the yield by around £0.2 billion a year.

  • The further 2 percentage point increase in all rates of property income tax is estimated to raise £0.4 billion a year on average from 2028-29. The costing of this policy includes small behavioural responses, reflecting additional tax-motivated incorporation and higher non-compliance, that reduce the yield by £0.1 billion a year. The potential long-term impact of the increase to property income tax rates and other related measures is discussed in paragraph 3.46.

Changes to dividend and capital gains taxation

3.18 The Budget includes the following changes to the dividend and capital gains tax (CGT) regimes:

  • Changes to the taxation framework for distributions from companies to individuals from April 2028 which is estimated to raise £0.8 billion by 2029-30. This introduces a number of changes to the system which aim to prevent company owners paying tax at lower CGT rates rather than at dividend income tax rates. The costing includes a significant reduction in the estimated yield over time to reflect the targeted tax base’s ability to plan to reduce the additional tax liability.

  • A reduction to the lifetime limit for the business asset disposal relief (BADR) from £1 million to £500,000 from April 2027 increases receipts by £0.3 billion in 2029-30. The introduction of a 10 per cent CGT rate for qualifying founders of high-growth or innovative companies from April 2027 reduces receipts in 2029-30 by £0.3 billion.

Other changes to taxes

3.19 This forecast also incorporates other changes to taxes which raise £1.1 billion in 2026-27, £1.3 billion in 2027-28, before falling to £0.2 billion by 2031-32. These include:

  • The Government has announced the abolition of the carbon price support (CPS) from April 2028 and provided funding for the Low Carbon Contracts Company (LCCC) enabling it to reduce contracts for difference (CfD) levies on billpayers. These measures cost an average £0.4 billion a year from 2027-28 onwards.[footnote 25] These measures are intended to offset the increase in electricity bills for non-energy-intensive-industry consumers due to the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (BICS) and an uplift to the Supercharger scheme.

  • In Budget 2025, fuel duty rates were frozen and the reversal of the 5p fuel duty cut delayed until September 2026. The Government has since announced a further freeze to fuel duty rates and delay of the reversal until January 2027, with this Budget extending these until June 2027. According to the latest policy, on 1 July 2027 the temporary five pence cut – first introduced in 2022 – will be reversed in full alongside an uprating of fuel duty rates. If implemented, it would lead to fuel duty rates rising from 52.95 pence per litre to 60.59 pence per litre. This policy costs £0.6 billion in 2026-27 and £0.8 billion in 2027-28. The reversal of the 5p cut has now been delayed five times and fuel duty has not been uprated with RPI since 2011. Paragraph 3.43 and Chapter 7 sets out the fiscal impacts if this latest iteration of fuel duty policy were to again not be implemented.

  • A cut to VAT on domestic electricity from 5 per cent to 0 per cent until April 2027 announced in July, with this Budget extending the cut until July 2027. This is expected to cost £0.7 billion in 2026-27 and £0.3 billion in 2027-28.

  • The Government has announced a package of temporary business rates measures through the remainder of the current valuation period, at a net cost of around £0.5 billion in 2028-29. These measures include a real-terms freeze in business rates liabilities for properties in certain sectors, increased reliefs for pubs and live music venues, and higher eligibility thresholds for small business rates relief. The Budget also extends existing schemes that limit increases in business rates bills following revaluation. The cost of these measures is partly offset by a two-year extension of the 1p transitional relief supplement.

  • The Budget also incorporates mayoral strategic authorities into the business rates retention system on a permanent basis. This increases the share of net business rates revenues flowing into local government by approximately £0.5 billion in 2031-32.[footnote 26] The measure means that a larger share of future growth in business rates revenues accrues to mayoral authorities rather than central government. This policy forms part of the Government’s wider devolution roadmap, which we discuss further in paragraph 3.38.

Measures impacting the Government’s balance sheet

3.20 The Government has increased the funding available for the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank (BBB) to invest in financial assets, such as loans and equity. This raises the Government’s financing requirement by £1.9 billion a year on average, and increases debt by £3.9 billion in 2031-32. The new investments are estimated to reduce borrowing by £0.5 billion in 2031-32, reflecting £0.6 billion of additional income, which is only slightly offset by expected losses due to loan write-offs and calls on guarantees. Taken together, the net impact of these measures is to increase debt by £3.4 billion in 2031-32.

3.21 The Government has also announced additional capacity for UK Export Finance (UKEF) to provide guarantees to back the purchases of British exports by foreign buyers. UKEF expects to issue a total of £40 billion of additional guarantees evenly between 2027-28 and 2030-31. This reduces borrowing by £0.2 billion a year over the medium-term but materially increases the public sector’s exposure to geopolitical risk. The £7 billion expansion of the Growth Guarantee Scheme offered by the BBB is expected to increase borrowing by £0.1 billion in 2026-27 and 2027-28 and £0.2 billion thereafter, reflecting the expected calls on the guarantees, which outweigh the fee income earned.

3.22 The ‘Your First Home’ Equity Loan Scheme will provide loans to first-time buyers of newbuild homes totalling £0.7 billion in 2027-28 and of £1 billion from 2028-29 onwards. This increases debt by £0.7 billion in the first year, thereafter the annual increase in debt from new loans is increasingly offset by loan repayments. We expect the scheme to only have a marginal impact on house prices and supply given its limited overall size.

Classification treatment of policies

3.25 On the advice of Treasury classification experts and pending an ONS decision on classification this section sets out how we are recording the following new Budget transactions:

  • Fees levied on landlords to register with local authorities are recorded as central government taxes and so increase receipts, while fees on developers to participate in the equity loans scheme are recorded as sales of goods and services and so decrease spending. These decisions do not affect borrowing or debt.

  • The introduction of timely payment for self assessment means that affected taxpayers make payments towards both their previous and current year liabilities during the transition year of 2029-30. These overlapping payments, together with the part reversal of the Budget 2025 measure that mandated coding out via the PAYE system, increase cash receipts in 2029-30 by £17 billion. As explained further in Chapter 6 the additional cash receipts reduce the CGNCR and public sector net debt in 2029-30, as both are measured in cash terms. We assume that the ONS will make an extraordinary accruals adjustment in 2029-30 to remove the temporary cash timing effect from these overlapping payments but will not do so in subsequent years.

3.26 The Treasury has also decided to switch the British Business Bank and National Housing Bank from departmental expenditure limits (DEL) to annually managed expenditure (AME).

Update on previous measures

3.27 We cannot review and re-cost all previous measures at each fiscal event, but we do look at those where the original (or revised) costings seem to be under- or over-performing, and costings that were identified as particularly uncertain.

3.28 The yield from the Budget 2025 measure to no longer exempt salary-sacrificed pension contributions from NICs, above an annual £2,000 threshold, has been revised up by an average of £0.4 billion in 2029-30 and 2030-31. This is driven by outturn data suggesting higher usage and average contributions than previously assumed and a stronger nominal earnings forecast.

3.29 In response to underperformance in the delivery model of their targeted case review (TCR) regime, DWP has decided to insource 2,500 FTE staff who were previously working for a third-party contractor to boost their productivity, as well as to hire an additional 900 FTE staff to undertake more case reviews. We included AME savings from this operational expansion in our pre-measures forecast. Despite the Government’s intention for these additional 900 staff to be permanent, we were informed after the closure of our pre-measures forecast that they would not be funding these staff beyond 2028-29. We will review both the resourcing and AME savings of this measure at our next forecast.

Update on previous indirect effects judgements

3.30 Together with the Treasury and departments responsible for implementation of the various policy measures, we have established transparent processes for monitoring and evaluation of the supply-side impacts of policies on potential output. We use these processes to check whether observed outcomes are consistent with the assumptions underpinning our economy forecast. We have made no explicit adjustments to the forecast as a result of monitoring and evaluation at this event. For larger policies, there is not yet evidence that their effects differ materially from those incorporated in our forecast, while policies experiencing delivery issues have relatively small effects in the forecast.

3.31 As set out in Chapter 2, in this forecast we have revised down our projection for new housing supply over the forecast period by 190,000. We have not, however, at this point revised our previous estimates of the positive contribution that the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) reforms would make to housing supply over this period. Instead, our assessment is related to the wider regulatory and fiscal environment and to sharp rises in construction costs. This illustrates the challenges associated with assessing the economic effects of regulatory policies, where the full range of relevant regulatory changes affecting any specific sector can be difficult to identify and quantify.[footnote 27] We will keep our NPPF assumption under review. A feasibility study for the evaluation of the NPPF reforms is expected from MHCLG in early 2027.

3.32 We have previously not included an assessment of the potential economic impacts of the Employment Rights Act 2025 (ERA), given it was dependent on ongoing consultations and secondary legislation. We have made an assessment at this event, following the conclusion of most of the consultations and the implementation of various components of the reforms. Our analysis suggests that the ERA will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses, particularly through increased uncertainty, lost flexibility and higher labour related costs, which will more than offset any potential positive impact on worker productivity.

3.33 However, the size of the impact of the ERA is highly uncertain, partly due to the difficulties mentioned above in assessing the economic effects of regulatory policy. It is likely that the negative impact from the final set of reforms is substantially less than the initial policy proposals put forward in 2024 would have been. There is also still some uncertainty about the final policy design of the zero-hour contract related measures. However, overall, we judge there is currently not clear evidence that this negative impact is above our 0.1 per cent potential output threshold, so we have not made an explicit adjustment to our forecast. We will keep this judgement under review.

3.34 The latest evidence on the increase in employer NICs announced at Autumn Budget 2024 does not suggest that its impacts have been materially different from our expectations. Sharper falls in employment among lower-paid sectors are consistent with our judgement that these firms would be most affected by the reduction of the secondary threshold and its interaction with the National Living Wage. That said, it remains too early to draw firm conclusions about the scale of the policy’s impacts relative to our original assumptions, given the wider effects impacting the labour market (see Chapter 2). A full evaluation is expected from HMRC in 2027.

3.35 At previous events we have incorporated estimates of the increase to labour supply from government employment support programmes. The extension to Talking Therapies, which we estimated would increase employment by 10,000 in our November 2023 forecast, was intended to increase both the number of completed treatments and the average number of sessions. However, this extension has not been delivered. Connect to Work, which we assumed – in our 2023 forecasts – would increase employment by around 25,000, aimed to help people with health conditions and disabilities into employment. The number of participants supported is now expected to be around a third lower than we assumed by 2028-29. These examples illustrate the challenges of making explicit adjustments to the economy forecast for departmental spending policies, given that the impacts are highly sensitive to subsequent changes to policy and operational design, possible reprioritisation of funding, delivery challenges, and wider changes to spending programmes which may have offsetting effects.[footnote 28]

3.36 The latest evidence on the expansion of 30 hours free childcare, suggests take-up has been stronger than expected. This was announced at Spring Budget 2023 and, as of June 2026, the number of active users of the offer was 17 per cent above the DfE target. This has increased spending on the policy relative to original expectations. However, higher take-up does not necessarily imply a larger labour supply effect – we originally estimated that this would increase employment by 60,000. Some parents receiving the additional support may have worked similar hours in its absence – particularly those on higher incomes – and it is possible that individuals earning above the £100k cut-off threshold have reduced their hours worked to receive the childcare benefit. The DfE evaluation for this policy is expected in 2027.

Policy risks

3.37 Our legislation requires that our forecasts reflect only current government policy. As such, when the Government sets out ‘policy ambitions’ or ‘intentions’, we ask the Treasury to confirm whether they represent firm policy. We use that information to determine what should be reflected in our forecast. Where they are not yet firm policy, we note them as a source of risk to our central forecast. A full database of risks to this forecast and the changes from previous updates will be available on our website.

3.38 The Government’s devolution roadmap sets out initial details of the transfer of powers and resources in England. This includes policies for local retention of income tax receipts from April 2028 and discretionary power for mayoral and foundation strategic authorities to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. We will incorporate any material economic and fiscal impacts of these reforms into our forecast once the detailed policy and implementation arrangements have been finalised.

3.39 The Timms Review of Personal Independence Payment and Milburn Report on youth, health, and employment have both published interim findings with final recommendations expected later this year. We will assess the economic and fiscal impacts of any resulting policy changes once the Government has responded and the policy details are sufficiently clear.

3.40 The Government has announced several future spending commitments following the end of the current Spending Review period. As discussed in paragraphs 5.16 to 5.19, this includes the Government’s commitment to reach 3.5 per cent of GDP spent on defence by 2035 and a commitment to significantly increase council house building. We will incorporate the economic and fiscal impacts of the final announcements made in these areas after the next Spending Review.

3.41 The Government has announced its intention to establish a National Care Service in England and has brought forward the Casey Commission’s recommendation on its design to 2027. The fiscal cost of these reforms is highly dependent on the final design of the reforms and the timing of their introduction. For example, the Health Foundation has previously estimated that reforms to social care could increase spending by between £3.5 billion and £17 billion a year, depending on the generosity and design of the system.[footnote 29] We will incorporate the economic and fiscal impacts once the detailed policy and funding arrangements have been confirmed. Based on the current policy regime, we projected in the 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability report that adult care spending in the UK would rise as a share of GDP from 1.2 per cent to 1.8 per cent over the next 50 years, largely reflecting demographic pressures associated with the UK’s projected growing old-age population. These spending pressures are expected to be most pronounced in the 2030s as the baby-boom cohort reaches their 80s, given the concentration of adult social care costs towards the end of life.

Extensions of temporary policies

3.42 The Budget includes several extensions to policies that are described as temporary and therefore not included in the forecast beyond the short term. This continues a pattern of such extensions at successive fiscal events. This introduces risk into the medium-term forecast which is produced on the basis of these temporary policies expiring.

3.43 At this Budget, fuel duty rates have again been frozen for a further 10 months until July 2027, from when the ‘temporary’ 5p cut to rates were first introduced at Spring Statement 2022.[footnote 30] The cumulative cost of freezing fuel duty rates between 2010-11 and 2027-28 and the 5p cut, relative to the stated policy that they will increase in line with RPI inflation, has risen to £139 billion. As shown in Table 7.1, if fuel duty were to remain frozen until 2029-30, public sector net borrowing would be £4.3 billion higher.

3.44 Other smaller measures which have been extended through repeated short-term policy decisions include various reliefs for business rates, the universal credit surplus earnings limit – which has been extended for the tenth consecutive year – and tariff suspension extensions.

The long-run impact of government policy

3.45 The Charter for Budget Responsibility requires us to assess the long-term impacts of new government policies, where these are material. We therefore report on new policies with long-run economic and fiscal impacts, especially where these differ from the effects that are expected to have occurred by the five-year timeframe at which we are required to produce our medium-term forecasts.

The long-run economic impact of measures

3.46 The 2 percentage point increase in property income tax rates in this Budget will be implemented on top of the 2 percentage point increase announced at Budget 2025. Both of these measures will come into force from April 2027 and represent a material reduction in returns to private landlords. This follows various measures over the past 10 years that have also reduced private landlord returns.[footnote 31] These measures collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents through two effects. First, potential landlords are less likely to enter the market, reducing long-run rental supply, which risks a steady long-term rise in rents if demand outstrips supply – which we think is more likely than not. Second, landlords are likely to pass on more of these costs to renters in the long-run through a combination of some current landlords leaving, thereby giving more price setting power to remaining landlords, and greater long-run flexibility to raise rents. Such rises in rents would offset at least some of the reduction in the commercial viability to landlords from the measures introduced in recent years.

3.47 The India-UK Free Trade Agreement could increase real GDP by amounts rising to 0.13 per cent by 2040, according to the Government’s impact assessment.[footnote 32] As these economic benefits are expected to build up gradually over the long-term, we do not make an explicit adjustment in the medium-term forecast. The UK is also currently negotiating with the EU on various policies, including sanitary and phytosanitary measures and alignment between the UK Emissions Trading Scheme and EU Emissions Trading System. The economic impact will depend on the outcome of these negotiations.

The long-run fiscal impact of measures

3.48 In our Fiscal risks and sustainability reports (FRS), we have highlighted the long-term costs of the triple lock policy which, under its current design, uprates the state pension each year by the greater of average earnings growth, CPI inflation, or 2.5 per cent. In the 2026 FRS long-term scenarios, an ageing population – combined with the triple lock – drove a significant projected increase in state pension spending from 5 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 9 per cent of GDP in 2075-76. We estimated that the triple lock accounted for around one third of this increase. In the FRS baseline long-term scenario, which assumes pensions are uprated by the triple lock, public sector debt is projected to reach 300 per cent of GDP by 2075. In a scenario where the state pension is instead assumed to be uprated by earnings each year, debt was projected to reach 260 per cent of GDP by 2075.

3.49 Under the adjusted triple lock system, which is expected to take effect from April 2030, the state pension will be uprated by the highest of CPI inflation, 2.5 per cent, or the increase required to maintain its value relative to earnings at 2029-30 levels. As a result, if the value of the state pension moves above its value relative to earnings in 2029-30 (due to periods in which inflation or 2.5 per cent is higher than earnings growth) then in subsequent periods (where earnings growth is higher than inflation or 2.5 per cent) it would converge back toward this relative value. This removes the so-called spending ratchet effect under the current triple lock whereby increases in pension values relative to earnings are permanently retained and compounded over time.

3.50 We have incorporated the adjusted triple lock into our central medium-term forecast from 2030-31 but it does not currently affect state pension costs over the forecast period.[footnote 33] However, the adjusted triple lock is likely to materially reduce the growth of state pension spending over the long term relative to the current triple lock. The exact long-term impact of this change will be highly dependent on the future relationship between earnings growth, inflation, and the 2.5 per cent floor. To illustrate this, Chart 3.4 applies earnings uprating, the current triple lock and the adjusted triple lock to historical outturn data for earnings and inflation since 1990. This shows that:

  • 1990-2007: Average earnings growth was typically above both inflation and 2.5 per cent.[footnote 34] As a result, the illustrative pension values under both the current triple lock and adjusted triple lock would have remained very close to those produced by earnings uprating alone.

  • 2008-2014: Inflation or 2.5 per cent consistently exceeded earnings growth. As such, pensions under both the current and adjusted triple lock would have been uprated by the same amount each year and seen their value relative to earnings rise.

  • 2015-2025: Earnings growth exceeded inflation or 2.5 per cent over seven of the 10 years. These are the years in which the current and adjusted triple lock mechanisms would have produced different pension value outcomes:

  1. under the current triple lock, pensions would be uprated by earnings growth in these years, maintaining the gaps with earnings indexation that develop when inflation or the 2.5 per cent targets bind. This illustrates the ratchet effect of the current triple lock, under which this gap can only widen over time.

  2. under the adjusted triple lock, pensions would instead have been uprated by inflation or 2.5 per cent in these years, narrowing the gap with earnings indexation. In a scenario where earnings continued to exceed inflation and 2.5 per cent in subsequent years, this gap would eventually close under the adjusted triple lock.

3.51 Over the period from 1990 to 2025, the adjusted triple lock would have produced annual outcomes relative to earnings growth and the current triple lock that varied significantly across the different economic environments described. Averaging over the period as a whole, state pension payments would have been on average 1.4 per cent lower each year than under the current triple lock and 4.4 per cent higher than under earnings uprating.

3.52 This analysis illustrates that while the adjusted triple lock will not eliminate the long-term cost of state pension uprating relative to earnings indexation, it is expected to reduce costs relative to the current triple lock. Provisional analysis based on the historical experience described above suggests that if the next 50 years looked similar to the last 35 years on average, the adjusted triple lock would reduce the projected long-term increase in debt by around 25 per cent of GDP in 2075-76 relative to retaining the current triple lock.[footnote 35] Debt would be around 10 per cent of GDP higher in the long-term than under an earnings uprating scenario, reflecting the likelihood that there would continue to be periods where the inflation or 2.5 per cent uprating mechanisms would bind.

The overall impact of these announcements on the long-term public finances therefore depends on the additional cost of the social care reform which, as discussed in paragraph 3.41, depends on the final policy design and the timing of its introduction.

Chapter 4: Public sector receipts

Summary of the receipts forecast

4.1 In the central forecast, total public sector receipts are projected to rise as a share of GDP from 40.1 per cent of GDP (£1.2 trillion) in 2025-26 to 42.9 per cent of GDP (£1.6 trillion) in 2031-32. Within this, as Chart 4.1 shows, National Accounts taxes as a share of GDP (the ‘tax take’) are forecast to increase sharply from 36.0 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 37.9 per cent of GDP in 2027-28, surpassing the previous historical high, before then rising more gradually to reach a peak of 38.6 per cent of GDP at the end of the forecast period.[footnote 36] This would be a 5.7 per cent of GDP increase on the pre-pandemic level of 32.9 per cent of GDP in 2019-20.

4.2 Table 4.1 details the main drivers of the expected 2.6 per cent of GDP increase in the tax take from 2025-26 to 2031-32. Increases in personal taxes (income tax and National Insurance contributions) contribute 1.6 per cent of GDP to this increase, reflecting forecast earnings growth, frozen personal tax thresholds until April 2031, and policy measures that raise self-assessment receipts. Capital taxes contribute 0.5 per cent of GDP to the increase due to projected rises in equity prices and the expected impact of inheritance tax and capital gains tax (CGT) policy changes largely announced in Autumn Budget 2024. Onshore corporation tax contributes a further 0.4 per cent of GDP to the increase mainly due to strong expected near-term profits growth.

4.3 Relative to our March 2026 forecast, National Accounts taxes as a share of GDP are forecast to be 0.2 per cent of GDP higher this year and just 0.1 per cent of GDP higher in 2030-31, as higher forecast receipts in nominal terms are almost offset by higher forecast nominal GDP. Of the rise in nominal receipts, around four-fifths of the increase in 2030-31 compared to March is due to changes in the underlying forecast, primarily due to a stronger nominal earnings forecast and higher forecast asset prices and profits. Around one-fifth is accounted for by the tax policy changes announced in this Budget.

4.11 In this forecast we expect public sector current receipts for the full year of 2026-27 to be £12 billion higher than forecast in March, which remains broadly consistent with the latest September cash receipts. Income tax (excluding self-assessed), NICs and onshore corporation tax receipts are expected to remain stronger than in our March forecast through the rest of the year as is the case in the September data. As outlined in Box 4.1, oil and gas revenues, which have been lower than expected up to August, are expected to recover in the remainder of the year due to the higher oil and gas prices. CGT receipts, mainly received in January 2027, are expected to be £5 billion higher than expected in March, reflecting an updated assessment of the strength in receipts seen in 2025-26 (paragraph 4.33). 4.12 Overall receipts in 2026-27 are expected to be relatively backloaded, with relatively more receipts expected in the final three months of 2026-27 than in a usual year. This is partly due to expected receipts from the Temporary Repatriation Facility introduced alongside reforms to the previous non-domiciled tax regime. As we set out when these reforms were announced, the estimated yield from this policy is highly uncertain.

Tax-by-tax analysis

Income tax (excluding self-assessed) and National Insurance contributions

4.13 Income tax (excluding self-assessed) and National Insurance contributions (NICs) are forecast to raise £520 billion (16.2 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, a 7.6 per cent increase from 2025-26. This rise is driven by strong nominal earnings growth combining with frozen tax thresholds. Receipts are then forecast to rise to £610 billion (16.5 per cent of GDP) in 2030-31, before remaining broadly flat as a share of GDP in 2031-32 as thresholds return to being uprated by CPI from April 2031. Almost all of this growth comes from higher PAYE income tax because it is a more progressive tax than NICs, and is therefore boosted by the freezes to tax thresholds. A further temporary increase is expected to income tax receipts between 2026-27 and 2028-29 due to the Temporary Repatriation Facility announced as part of previous reforms to the non-domiciled regime.

4.14 Budget 2025 extended the allowances and threshold freezes in income tax and NICs to April 2031, meaning the majority will be frozen for most of the 2020s. This increases the sensitivity of the receipts forecast to nominal earnings changes through ‘fiscal drag’. Using our standard ready reckoners, a 1 percentage point increase in nominal earnings and CPI would raise income tax and NICs receipts by an average of £7 billion a year under the current policy of frozen thresholds to April 2031. This is around £2.5 billion a year higher than if thresholds were increasing with CPI, reflecting the additional fiscal drag generated.[footnote 41] This is also likely to have an adverse effect on financial work incentives by increasing the marginal tax rate on each additional hour of work. Following our standard approach, we have estimated that, taken together, the threshold freezes in income tax and NICs from 2022-23 to 2030-31 could decrease labour supply by 215,000 in average-hours equivalent (AHE) terms by 2030-31.[footnote 42]

4.15 Table 4.3 shows that relative to the March forecast, non-SA income tax and NICs receipts are expected to be £9 billion higher in 2026-27. This reflects the higher-than-expected PAYE receipts received so far this year, which has likely been driven by nominal earnings slowing by less than expected compared with the March forecast. Nominal earnings growth has been particularly strong in the public sector, in part due to the earlier timing of pay awards compared with previous years that may have boosted receipts against our previously assumed profile for receipts in 2026-27. Over the rest of the forecast, receipts are expected to be £8 billion higher, on average, than expected in March. This is driven by the higher outturn this year and a higher forecast for nominal earnings growth next year, which are only partly offset by a weaker forecast for the number of employees and the effects of Government decisions in 2029-30 and 2030-31.

4.16 The main effect of Budget policy decisions is through the measure to introduce timely payment for self-assessment and part reversal of the Budget 2025 measure that mandated coding out via the PAYE system, explained in more detail in paragraph 3.13. This transfers receipts from PAYE to SA IT that were previously associated with the coding out measure. The indirect effects of policy decisions have a very small downward impact on receipts in most years.

Self-assessed income tax

4.17 Self-assessed income tax (SA IT) is forecast to raise £63 billion in 2026-27 (2.0 per cent of GDP), a 17.2 per cent increase on 2025-26.
