Receipts are then forecast to rise to £94 billion (2.5 per cent of GDP) in 2031-32, driven by further expected receipts from the non-domiciled tax regime reforms, the reclassification of carried interest into SA IT from CGT, and policy measures announced at this Budget.

4.18 Table 4.4 shows that compared to March, SA IT receipts are £1.0 billion lower in 2026-27 but higher thereafter by increasing amounts, peaking at £11 billion in 2030-31. The pre-measures forecast changes reflect a stronger profits forecast boosting dividend income, and the impact of higher equity prices on the carried interest forecast. This is estimated to increase accrued SA IT receipts by £3.5 billion in 2029-30 and £6.5 billion in 2030-31. Paragraph 3.25 provides further detail on the accounting treatment of this measure. The modernisation of the distributions framework is estimated to increase SA IT receipts by around £2 billion in 2029-30 and 2030-31, partially offset by the expected reduction in CGT receipts from this measure. Oil and gas receipts

4.26 Offshore corporation tax, petroleum revenue tax (PRT), and the energy profits levy (EPL) are expected to raise £5.1 billion (0.2 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, a 25 per cent increase on 2025-26 due to higher oil and gas prices. Oil and gas receipts are then expected to fall over the remainder of the forecast, as the recent rises in energy prices are expected to unwind, down to £1.9 billion by 2028-29. Receipts are then forecast to decline further to £0.3 billion in 2030-31 and close to zero in 2031-32, primarily due to the expiry of the EPL in September 2029 and the expected continued fall in oil and gas production.

4.27 These forecasts are based on the North Sea Transition Authority’s (NSTA) projection for total oil and gross gas production, shown in Chart 4.6. This shows that production has been declining since the start of the 2000s and that this decline is expected to continue at around 10 per cent a year over 2027 to 2031. The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the NSTA’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries.[footnote 43] The forecast annual pace of decline would be around 14 per cent a year if there were no production from any new fields.

Source: NSTA, OBR

4.28 Relative to our March forecast, oil and gas receipts are expected to be £2.6 billion higher in 2026-27, largely due to significantly higher oil and gas prices. However, the increase has been partly offset by the latest assessment of the impact on receipts of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity, described in Box 4.1. Receipts from the energy profits levy are now expected to be £9 billion in total between 2026-27 and 2030-31, up from £2.5 billion at the March forecast. The EPL is now expected to remain in place until September 2029, when the Energy Security Investment Mechanism (ESIM) is expected to trigger based on anticipated average oil and gas prices. This is two years later than in the March forecast.

Box 4.1: The impact of mergers and acquisitions on oil and gas revenues

Recent merger activity by firms operating in the UK continental shelf has resulted in companies with a large stock of tax losses combining operations with tax-paying companies, allowing greater use of losses against taxable profits. The 2021 to 2023 period saw expansion of larger and mid-sized oil and gas companies, outside of the major international groups. Since 2024, several of these companies have merged with portfolios held by major international companies.

The impact of this activity was a key factor behind the downward revision to our November 2025 forecast for offshore corporation taxa and in this forecast has muted the upward impact on receipts this year of higher oil and gas prices. Our tax forecasts are generated by HMRC’s North Sea microsimulation model, which captures M&A activity by combining information on company ownership of fields and tax returns data. The mergers in 2025 and 2026 had a similar pattern of dampening the receipts forecasts in both this and the November 2025 forecast, largely through making the stock of historical losses more readily accessible to profitable companies.

The left panel of Chart A shows the impact on losses used of the mergers incorporated at this forecast. The blue bars show the change in losses used due to recently completed mergers, which increase by a net £2.7 billion between 2026 and 2031. The frontloaded pattern reflects the assumption that, once historical losses become accessible, they are used as quickly as possible. Higher oil and gas prices in the early part of the forecast also generate more profits against which the losses can be used. This frontloading of loss utilisation results in a faster rundown of the stock of outstanding losses, leaving fewer losses available for use in the later years of the forecast.

The forecast also includes an assumption that a further 20 per cent of the stock of losses become accessible from possible future mergers.b The impact of this, shown by the yellow bars, is to increase losses used by £2.2 billion between 2026 and 2031.

The right panel shows the impact on receipts from the greater losses used, which mirrors this pattern, with greater reductions in the early years of the forecast when more losses are available against taxable profits. The net impact between 2026-27 and 2031-32 is a reduction of £1.3 billion from completed mergers and £0.8 billion from the adjustment for future mergers.

Road taxes

4.29 Fuel duty is expected to raise £24 billion (0.8 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, which is £0.6 billion less than in 2025-26, largely due to higher pump prices reducing demand. Relative to the March forecast, receipts are expected to be £0.7 billion lower this year mostly due to policy changes and lower demand. In May 2026, the Government announced that fuel duty rates would remain unchanged until January 2027. In this Budget, the Government has announced that rates will remain unchanged until July 2027 at which point the 5p cut first implemented in March 2022 will be unwound and then uprated by RPI. Receipts are then forecast to increase by £1.8 billion (7 per cent) in 2027-28 and by £0.9 billion in 2028-29 assuming this policy is implemented.

4.30 On the assumption that the latest policy is implemented, fuel duty receipts are forecast to peak in nominal terms at £27 billion (0.8 per cent of GDP) in 2028-29 before falling by around £2.1 billion by 2031-32. This reflects the turning point when the additional revenue from the assumed increase in fuel duty rates is forecast to be outweighed by the declining tax base due to a rising electric vehicle (EV) share. Chart 4.7 shows that in practice fuel duty revenues have been consistently lower than forecast. This is largely because despite successive policy commitments to raise fuel duty rates, they have not actually been increased since 2011-12. If the duty rate were to again remain unchanged at its current level throughout the forecast period it would reduce receipts, on average, by £4 billion a year between 2027-28 and 2031-32.

4.31 Vehicle excise duty (VED) receipts are expected to be £9 billion (0.3 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, a 6 per cent increase compared to 2025-26 driven by an increase in vehicle registrations. Across the forecast period, receipts are expected to increase in each successive year, rising to £14 billion by the forecast horizon. Capital taxes

4.32 Capital gains tax (CGT) is forecast to raise £26 billion (0.8 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, around a 5 per cent increase from 2025-26. Receipts are then forecast to rise to £41 billion in 2031-32 (1.1 per cent of GDP), largely driven by a forecast of rising equity prices.

4.33 Relative to the March forecast, before the impact of policy measures, CGT receipts are expected to be £4.8 billion higher this year largely due to a revised assessment of the forestalling of receipts in 2025-26, which is explained below.[footnote 44] Thereafter, CGT receipts are forecast to be higher than the March forecast by an average of £3.1 billion each year, driven by the 2025-26 receipts reassessment and the impact of higher forecast equity prices. The Budget 2026 policy to reform the taxation framework for distributions from companies to individuals is estimated to reduce CGT receipts by £1.2 billion in 2031-32. However, this is more than offset by the expected increase in SA income tax receipts from this measure. The net impact of the new Founders’ Relief and the lower Business Asset Disposal Relief lifetime limit reduce receipts by an average of £0.1 billion a year from 2027-28.

4.34 CGT receipts for 2025-26, which largely relate to 2024-25 asset disposals, were 78 per cent higher than the previous year. This was partly due to forestalling – an increase in the disposal of assets in 2024-25 ahead of anticipated CGT policy rate increases at Autumn Budget 2024. In the March 2026 forecast, we made a judgement that £4.3 billion of liabilities were brought forward due to this forestalling. This assumption was based on the average magnitude of forestalling seen ahead of anticipated policy changes before Budget 2021 and ahead of rate changes in 2010. We assumed that £1.1 billion of these forestalled liabilities related to transactions that would have taken place later in that same year, resulting in a net £3.2 billion of additional liabilities in the 2024-25 tax year.

4.35 HMRC have since reviewed this forestalling assumption using a more detailed analysis of the pattern of asset disposals across the year.[footnote 45] Compared with a ‘normal’ CGT tax year, the distribution of disposals in 2024-25 suggests that around £5.8 billion of CGT liabilities were brought forward due to forestalling. The analysis also suggests that a higher proportion of these forestalled liabilities than previously assumed were likely to have been brought forward from later in that year (£4.3 billion), because the pattern of disposals later in the year was relatively weak compared to previous years. This suggests there was a net £1.5 billion of additional disposed liabilities in the 2024-25 tax year due to forestalling. The larger in-year unwinding increases the estimate for structural disposals in 2024-25. This, alongside the subsequent lower unwinding, boosts the forecast for disposals and receipts in the next three years compared to March.

4.36 CGT is one of the most volatile and therefore uncertain tax streams. This is reflected in the average size of the difference between CGT forecasts and outturn. Over the last ten forecasts, the one-year ahead CGT average absolute forecast difference was 24.5 per cent of forecast, compared with 4.3 per cent for total public sector current receipts.[footnote 46] Revenues are sensitive to movements in asset prices, in particular equity prices (see Box 3.1 in the March 2026 EFO), which are typically highly volatile from year to year. In addition, receipts are highly sensitive to behavioural decisions made by a relatively narrow group of higher net worth taxpayers, who often have flexibility in choosing when to dispose of assets in response to changes in asset value or to policy changes.

4.37 Property transaction taxes are forecast to raise £17 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, a 0.6 per cent decline relative to 2025-26. This is driven by the share of year-to-date receipts in 2026-27 implying a lower annual total for the year compared to 2025.26.The recent fall in house prices in areas of London and the South East, where the level of property prices are higher than the national average, partly informs this judgement. Given the progressivity of the stamp duty land tax system, this has a relatively large effect on overall receipts. Receipts are then forecast to rise gradually to £26 billion (0.7 per cent of GDP) in 2031-32, driven by rising property transactions and house prices over the remainder of the forecast period.

4.38 Relative to the March forecast, property transaction tax receipts are expected to be around £3.2 billion lower in 2026-27 and an average of £3.9 billion a year lower over the rest of the forecast. Changes are largely due to the lower-than-expected in-year receipts for both residential and commercial sectors and reductions to the forecasts for house prices and property transactions.

4.39 Inheritance tax (IHT) receipts are forecast to raise £9 billion (0.3 per cent of GDP) in 2026-27, a 7.2 per cent increase on last year. Receipts are expected to continue to increase over the forecast, reaching £15 billion (0.4 per cent of GDP) in 2031-32, driven by rising equity and house prices, a growing proportion of UK deaths subject to inheritance tax, and the impact of policies announced in Autumn Budget 2024. Relative to the March forecast, IHT receipts are expected to be £0.5 billion lower on average, in every year of the forecast, largely driven by lower in-year outturn which is partly offset by higher equity prices.

4.40 An increasing proportion of IHT revenue is forecast to come from changes to the inheritance tax regime announced at and since Autumn Budget 2024, including taxing inherited pension pots and introducing changes to agricultural and business property reliefs, which account for around one-sixth of total revenue by the end of the forecast. The behavioural responses to these measures and the tax base for inheritable pension wealth are particularly uncertain.

Business rates

4.41 Business rates are expected to raise £35 billion in 2026-27, a 4.5 per cent increase relative to 2025-26. Business rates bills are calculated by multiplying the rateable value by the multiplier (which is typically uprated by CPI inflation) less reliefs for which the property is eligible. Growth in 2026-27 reflects several changes in the business rates system that took effect in April 2026. These include a revaluation in which the rateable values of non-domestic property were updated, a neutral change to multipliers with a lower rate for retail, hospitality and leisure properties and a higher rate for high-value properties and several temporary measures to cap bill increases resulting from the revaluation.

4.42 The 2026-27 estimate for business rates in England is based on forecast information from local authorities which was not available when we finalised the March forecast. This indicates that receipts this year will be £2 billion lower than previously assumed. Over the rest of the forecast period, the higher path for CPI inflation pushes up the multiplier, adding around £1 billion to the business rates forecast by 2030-31. This leaves business rates little changed from our March forecast by that year. In this Budget, the Government has announced a number of further measures which reduce business rates charged on properties in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors, which lower receipts by £0.4 billion in 2027-28 and £0.6 billion in 2028-29.

Excise duties

4.43 Alcohol duty receipts are expected to raise £13 billion in 2026-27, a 2.7 per cent increase relative to 2025-26. Receipts are then anticipated to increase to £14 billion by 2031-32, driven by increases to the duty rate that offset an assumed average 1 per cent decline in alcohol consumption in each year. Compared to the March forecast, we assume a lower consumption trend, reflecting recent outturns, that reduces forecast receipts by an average of £0.2 billion each year.

4.44 Tobacco duty receipts are expected to raise £7 billion in 2026-27, a 1 per cent decrease relative to 2025-26, as higher duty rates only partly offset falling consumption. Receipts then fall to £6 billion by 2031-32 as consumption continues to decline. Vaping duty, effective from October 2026, raises £0.2 billion in 2026-27 and £0.7 billion by 2031-32. Compared to the March forecast, tobacco receipts are broadly unchanged.

4.45 Betting and gaming receipts are expected to raise £5 billion in 2026-27, a 31 per cent increase relative to 2025-26, driven by the increase to tax rates on remote gambling announced at Budget 2025. Thereafter, receipts are forecast to grow by an average of 3.4 per cent a year to £6 billion in 2031-32. Compared to the March forecast, before the impact of policy measures, receipts are higher by an average of £0.2 billion. This is largely due to stronger-than-expected remote gaming duty receipts, suggesting a slower-than-expected reduction in activity in response to the rate increase. The increase to machine gaming rates announced at this Budget increases receipts by a further estimated £0.1 billion a year from 2027-28.

Other taxes

4.46 VAT refunds are forecast to cost £31 billion in 2026-27, a 2.7 per cent increase from 2025-26. Repayments then grow over the forecast in line with government consumption, reaching £36 billion by 2031-32. Relative to our March forecast, refunds are higher across the forecast period, by £0.1 billion in 2026-27 before rising to £0.5 billion in 2030-31. This is due to strength in outturn data feeding through the forecast, particularly for local authorities. VAT refunds are offset by spending and are neutral for public sector borrowing.

4.47 Environmental levies are expected to total £14 billion in 2026-27, rising to a forecast £16 billion by 2031-32. This is due to an increase in electricity supply and generation in the capacity market and contracts for difference (CfD) forecasts, and an expected £1.1 billion increase from Sizewell C regulated asset base (RAB) levy receipts. Compared to the March forecast, environmental levies are on average £1.2 billion lower each year. This is mostly due to lower CfD receipts reflecting the Government’s decision to provide funding to reduce CfD levies on billpayers (see paragraph 3.19), the near-term rise in wholesale electricity prices, and project delays reducing electricity generation. Receipts relating to the capacity market scheme are lower towards the forecast horizon due to lower-than-expected prices at recent auctions. Most receipts from environmental levies are directly offset in spending because they are used to provide subsidies for energy generators. This means they are generally neutral for public sector borrowing.

4.48 Council tax receipts are expected to raise £54 billion in 2026-27, a 7 per cent increase from 2025-26 driven largely by increases in the rates of council tax in England, Scotland and Wales. Receipts are then forecast to rise to £70 billion by 2031-32 as both council tax rates and the number of households are assumed to grow. Receipts are broadly unchanged from our March forecast. Council tax receipts are directly offset by local authority spending and so they are neutral for public sector borrowing. For more information on the council tax rebate announced at this Budget, see paragraph 3.11 in Chapter 3.

4.49 Home Office fees are forecast to raise £6 billion in 2026-27, a 2.5 per cent increase on 2025-26. Relative to our March forecast, receipts are £0.3 billion lower in 2026-27 due to lower-than-expected immigration health surcharge receipts. Thereafter, overall receipts are on average £0.2 billion higher in every year due to higher projected total in-country work visas, which is partly offset by our lower net migration forecast.

Other receipts

4.50 Interest and dividend receipts are forecast to raise £44 billion in 2026-27, a 7.2 per cent increase on 2025-26. Receipts then rise throughout the forecast, driven mainly by interest received from funded public sector pensions and accrued interest on student loans. Receipts are forecast to be higher than expected in March by around £3 billion in 2027-28 and 2028-29. This reflects higher inflation increasing accrued interest on student loans and higher interest rates boosting returns on public sector assets, deposits and reserves. By 2030-31, receipts return to the level assumed in the March forecast, driven by changes to the assumed rate of return on funded pension assets and inflation subsiding.

4.51 Gross operating surplus (GOS) is the sum of general government depreciation and public corporations’ (PCs’) operating surplus and is projected to reach £86 billion in 2026-27, rising to £105 billion by the forecast horizon. Relative to March, GOS is expected to be an average of £0.6 billion a year higher. General government depreciation is expected to rise from £69 billion in 2026-27 to £87 billion in 2031-32. This is £0.8 billion higher in 2026-27 than expected in March, with the difference rising to £2.7 billion in 2030-31. This is mostly due to higher depreciation rates in outturn, which we assume will persist throughout the forecast. Depreciation is offset by spending and is neutral for public sector borrowing. Changes in PC operating surplus since March largely reflect revisions to the outturn.

Chapter 5: Public sector expenditure

Summary of the expenditure forecast

5.1 As Chart 5.1 shows, in the central forecast, public spending is expected to increase from 44.5 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 45.7 per cent of GDP in 2027-28, before gradually declining to 44.7 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. This would be 5.5 percentage points higher than the pre-pandemic level in 2019-20, and 5.0 percentage points higher compared to the pre-financial crisis level of spending in 2006-07.

5.2 As shown in Table 5.1, the change in public spending over the forecast period (2026-27 to 2031-32) is the result of changes in both departmental expenditure limits (DEL), which fall as a share of GDP in every year of the forecast, and annually managed expenditure (AME), which is forecast to peak in 2027-28 before falling gradually until 2030-31:

  • Departmental expenditure limits are expected to rise as a share of GDP from 21.1 per cent in 2025-26 to 21.5 per cent in 2026-27 before gradually falling to 20.0 per cent by 2031-32. The planned fall in the later years of the forecast is explained by decreases in both day-to-day spending (resource DEL or RDEL) from 16.9 per cent of GDP to 16.3 per cent of GDP between 2027-28 and 2031-32, and in capital spending (capital DEL or CDEL) which falls from 4.0 per cent of GDP in 2027-28 to 3.7 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. After the end of the current Spending Review period, these projections are based on assumptions set by the Government for overall total RDEL and CDEL, rather than on detailed departmental spending plans. As set out later in this chapter, there are significant pressures on departmental spending over this period.

  • Annually managed expenditure is expected to rise as a share of GDP from 23.4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 24.9 per cent in 2027-28, then fall to 24.4 per cent by 2030-31, before rising again in 2031-32 to 24.6 per cent. Welfare spending and debt interest spending both rise from 2025-26 to 2027-28, and then are broadly stable until rising slightly again in 2031-32. There are forecast declines from 2027-28 in locally financed expenditure and in other areas of AME spending, as payments from compensation schemes decline and the deficit in unfunded public sector pension schemes falls as a share of GDP.

5.3 Chart 5.1 shows that total public spending as a share of GDP is higher in the near term relative to the March 2026 forecast. The difference then narrows so that the latest forecast is only slightly higher in 2030-31 at 44.6 per cent of GDP, compared to the 44.3 per cent of GDP forecast in March. These near-term increases are mainly driven by higher forecast spending on debt interest and welfare, explained in more detail later in this chapter.

Changes in spending since the March 2026 forecast

5.6 Table 5.2 shows that spending is forecast to rise by £31 billion a year on average over the forecast period compared to the March 2026 forecast. The main drivers of this increase include:

  • Underlying forecast differences, which increase spending by £27 billion a year on average. This is primarily driven by debt interest spending which is £14 billion higher a year on average across the forecast period, largely due to higher Bank Rate and gilt rate expectations. Higher CPI uprating increases welfare spending by £5 billion a year on average. Changes in the local authority net spending and public corporations’ capital expenditure forecasts described in paragraphs 5.26 and 5.32 further increase spending by £4 billion a year on average.

  • PSNB-neutral forecast differences, which are offset in receipts, raise spending by £1.3 billion a year on average.

  • The direct effect of Government decisions announced in this Budget increases borrowing across the first five years of the forecast by £3.3 billion a year on average, driven largely by higher defence spending. The largely offsetting effects on DEL and AME of the unfunded pensions valuation are discussed in more detail in paragraphs 5.8 and 5.32. Spending policy decisions are described in more detail in Chapter 3.

  • The indirect effects of Government decisions announced in this Budget increase spending by £0.1 billion a year on average. This mainly reflects higher debt interest from the near-term increase in borrowing due to policy, and a reduced departmental underspend judgement in 2027-28. These effects are partly offset by lower benefit uprating due to some policy measures slightly reducing inflation.

Analysis of expenditure by category

Spending within departmental expenditure limits (DEL)

5.7 As set out in Table 5.1, spending subject to departmental expenditure limits makes up almost half of all public spending. The current spending review period runs to 2028-29 for resource, and 2029-30 for capital spending. As stated in paragraph 5.2, beyond these years there are no detailed departmental spending plans and so our forecast is based on assumptions for total resource and capital spending that are set by the Government. In line with the Charter for Budget Responsibility, the next spending review will take place in 2027 and set DEL budgets for a minimum of three years. In the rest of this section, ‘RDEL spending’ refers to departmental resource, or day-to-day, spending, and ‘CDEL spending’ refers to departmental capital, or investment, spending.[footnote 47] Total DEL (or TDEL) is the sum of both RDEL and CDEL.

5.8 When analysing spending in real terms (that is, adjusted for the GDP deflator) over the forecast and when comparing real growth rates between this forecast and the last we have made the following adjustments:

  • We have removed from the October 2026 forecast the reductions to RDEL related to the 2024 valuation of unfunded public service pension schemes. The Government Actuary’s Department recommended a lower employer contribution rate in the valuation reports published thus far, primarily because of increases to the discount (‘SCAPE’) rate.[footnote 48] Employer pension contribution rates are reduced from 2027-28, providing savings to departments, and the government has correspondingly reduced RDEL by £16 billion a year. The lower pension contributions act to increase net spending and increase AME by a similar amount to the reduction in RDEL, making these changes broadly neutral for overall spending.[footnote 49] The unfunded pensions forecast is covered in more detail in paragraph 5.32.

  • We have restated the March 2026 forecast for classification changes between DEL and AME made at this forecast. For RDEL, this includes the switch of central government subsidies to public corporations,[footnote 50] and business rates under-indexation compensation and relief grants from AME to DEL,[footnote 51] which increase RDEL by an average of £3.3 billion over the forecast period. For CDEL, the switch of the British Business Bank from DEL to AME decreases CDEL by an average of £0.1 billion over the forecast period. [footnote 52]

5.9 In cash terms, total departmental spending (TDEL) is forecast to rise over the forecast period to reach £762 billion in 2031-32, with RDEL set to reach £621 billion and CDEL £141 billion, as shown in Table 5.4. As shown in Table 5.3 and Chart 5.4 by the dotted line, in real terms and excluding the adjustments above, RDEL spending is set to grow by an average 1.1 per cent over the forecast period, with fastest growth this year at 2.8 per cent. If we include the reduction in RDEL due to the 2024 valuation changes (the solid blue line in Chart 5.4), the real rate of growth of RDEL is on average 0.7 per cent. Real CDEL spending is set to grow at a rate of 0.4 per cent on average over the forecast. Within this there are real-terms reductions forecast in the next three years from 2027-28 to 2029-30, and an assumption of on average 0.9 per cent growth in the final two years of the forecast.

Departmental spending allocations in 2026-27

5.10 As Table 5.4 shows, RDEL is now forecast to be £555 billion in 2026-27, an increase on our March forecast of £7.2 billion. This difference is made up of:

  • Policy measures which have increased spending by £5.5 billion in 2026-27 – primarily a £2.6 billion council tax rebate and a £2.1 billion increase in defence spending.

  • A set of reclassifications of AME spending into DEL (as set out in paragraph 5.8) have overall increased DEL spending by an estimated £3.3 billion.

  • These are partially offset by our judgement that overall departments will underspend their resource budgets by a larger amount (£3.5 billion) than our previous March forecast (£1.8 billion), based on our assessment of the most recent spending outturn data so far this year.

5.11 The lower panel of Table 5.4 shows that CDEL is now forecast to be £128 billion in 2026-27 which is a £5.2 billion increase on our March forecast. This difference is almost entirely a reduction in our underspend judgement, which increases spending by £5.2 billion. We now expect that departments will underspend their capital budgets by £4.5 billion, compared to the £9.7 billion we estimated in March. Capital underspends were lower than we expected in 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 and departments have spent a higher-than-average proportion of capital than expected at this point in the year.[footnote 53] Lower underspends may indicate departments have become better able to spend their budgets during periods of fast real growth in capital spending than was the case in the past.[footnote 54]

Departmental spending allocations in the rest of the Spending Review period

5.12 As shown in the top panel of Table 5.4, RDEL is expected to increase by £18 billion over the remaining two years of the Spending Review period (2027-28 to 2028-29), to reach £573 billion by 2028-29. This is £9 billion lower than we expected in the March 2026 forecast, with the main changes due to:

  • Policy changes, including the reduction in RDEL to reflect lower employer pension contributions, which lower RDEL spending by an average of £13 billion a year. Excluding the pension change, RDEL policies increase spending by an average £3.0 billion, primarily reflecting higher defence funding.

  • Classification changes increasing the forecast by an average £1.8 billion.

  • Forecast changes reflecting updated estimates of the composition of DEL, with more included as fiscal spending, further increase spending by an average £0.7 billion.

  • An increase in our underspend judgement in 2028-29 reflecting the spending pressures discussed in more detail below.

5.13 As shown in the lower panel of Table 5.4, CDEL is expected to increase by £6.0 billion over the remaining three years of the Spending Review period for capital spending, to reach £134 billion by 2029-30. Compared to the March 2026 forecast capital spending is on average forecast to be £1.4 billion lower over this period, with the main changes due to:

  • Policy changes which reduce spending by an average of £1.5 billion a year. These are primarily reductions to departmental capital budgets announced as part of the funding for the defence investment plan.

  • Small changes to the underspend judgements on average reduce spending by £0.3 billion to reflect lower pressures on capital budgets, and small classification changes reduce spending by an average of £0.1 billion. Both are offset by forecast updates taking on revised estimates of the composition of DEL, which increase spending by an average £0.5 billion.

Pressures in the Spending Review period

5.14 There are some significant pressures on departmental spending limits over the remainder of the Spending Review. Particular risks include:

  • Higher-than-expected inflation reduces the real spending power of departments as DEL budgets are set in cash terms. Based on the increase in inflation in this forecast compared to the March 2026 forecast, nominal spending would need to be on average £2 billion higher in each year of the Spending Review to maintain the real value of departmental spending plans. Compared to the inflation forecast in March 2025, when the current Spending Review envelope was set, nominal spending plans would need to be on average £7 billion higher in each year than the original Spending Review envelopes to maintain the real value of departmental spending plans.

  • Central government spending on public sector pay makes up around 40 per cent of total RDEL. If all pay settlements were on average 1 per cent higher than expected this would increase public sector pay spending by around £2 billion per year. Higher inflation increases the general risk that there will be pressure for higher pay settlements than anticipated when budgets were set.

  • Efficiency savings: as part of the 2025 Spending Review, the Government published departmental efficiency plans, with the aim of delivering £14 billion in annual efficiency savings by 2028-29.[footnote 55] Some past efficiency programmes have not delivered the initially expected levels of savings.[footnote 56] If this were to be the case again then this would place further pressure on spending envelopes.

  • Other pressures: some specific areas of spending where cost pressures could be significantly higher or lower than expected include:

  • Special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) provision, where the number of children with education, health and care plans (EHCP) increased by 12.5 per cent between January 2025 and January 2026. While data suggests growth in referrals has slowed over the same period, the impact that the reforms announced in February 2026 will have on spending in this area remains very uncertain.[footnote 57] Elsewhere within schools the falling number of pupils in secondary schools could reduce pressures on school spending if it results in a reduction in the number of schools and teachers.[footnote 58]

  • Accommodation for asylum seekers, where the number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support has fallen by 12 per cent between June 2025 and June 2026, and at 90,000 is 25 per cent below the September 2023 peak of 120,000.[footnote 59] The numbers of asylum claims, and detected illegal arrivals, were 5,000 (6 per cent) and 500 (16 per cent) lower in 2025-26 compared to 2024-25, suggesting the number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support will fall further if the Government can maintain the current level of claim processing. The implications for local government spending is discussed in paragraph 5.27.

  • Prisons and wider justice system, where the Government’s response to capacity pressures on prisons through the early prisoner release scheme could increase costs in probation services given existing staffing shortages estimated at 3,150 sentence management staff in 2026-27[footnote 60] mean the marginal cost of expanding these services will be high. There are additional pressures in courts with crown case backlogs standing at around 80,000 and open tribunal cases reaching the highest level since 2012-13 at 860,000.[footnote 61] [footnote 62]

5.15 There is a particular risk to RDEL spending plans in 2028-29 because they are due to be reconsidered in the next spending review. Historically, the real growth of RDEL has typically been higher than originally planned in the final year covered in overlapping Spending Reviews. Based on our assessment of these and wider pressures, at this event we assume that departments will not underspend against existing RDEL plans in 2028-29. This follows the judgement made in our November 2025 forecast to reduce the underspend assumption in 2028-29 to account for pressures from SEND spending. We have kept our underspend assumptions largely unchanged for CDEL.

Departmental spending after the Spending Review period

5.16 Following the end of the Spending Review period, the Government provides an overall assumption for total resource and capital spending for the remainder of the forecast:

  • Total departmental resource spending is assumed to reach £620 billion by the end of the forecast, implying average annual real terms growth of 0.8 per cent over these three years. In the final year of the forecast, the real-terms growth rate is reduced to 0.7 per cent, a reduction of £5.5 billion to the pre-measures spending assumption of keeping RDEL constant as a share of GDP.

  • Total departmental capital spending is assumed to reach £140 billion by 2031-32, implying real terms growth of 0.9 per cent in the final two years of the forecast.

5.17 To illustrate the spending implications of these assumed envelopes, we consider what commitments in some areas of spending imply for growth in spending in areas not covered by commitments, often called ‘unprotected’ spending. In terms of day-to-day departmental spending (RDEL), we assume the following:

  • Spending on the NHS grows at 2.6 per cent a year in real terms after 2028-29, in line with growth rates set at the 2025 Spending Review.

  • Spending on defence is expected to rise from 2.6 per cent of GDP in 2026-27 to 2.7 per cent of GDP in 2029-30, and to then rise to 3.0 per cent of GDP in 2030-31 and to 3.1 per cent of GDP in 2031-32, in line with the Government’s Defence Investment Plan and its commitment announced at this Budget to reach 3.5 per cent of GDP in 2035. The total additional 0.9 per cent of GDP on defence spending in 2035-36 would represent around £35 billion in 2026-27 terms. We assume that the fraction of NATO-qualifying defence spending that is spent on day-to-day expenditure within the RDEL envelope is held constant to that planned in 2029-30.

  • Spending on Official Development Assistance (ODA) grows in line with gross national income (GNI) after 2028-29, in line with the Government’s commitment to spend 0.3 per cent of GNI on ODA by 2027.

  • Underlying spending on special educational needs (SEND) grows by 0.4 per cent a year in real terms reflecting the Treasury’s stated assumption, and spending on the remaining core mainstream schools budget is held flat per pupil in real terms as a policy-neutral baseline.

5.18 Within the assumed envelope for total RDEL spending provided by the Treasury, these assumptions would leave other ‘unprotected’ RDEL spending (accounting for just over a quarter of day-to-day departmental spending) falling by 2.6 per cent a year in real terms in the final three years of the forecast. Spending would have to be £11 billion higher in 2031-32 for unprotected spending not to fall in real terms from 2028-29. As outlined in Box 4.2 in the March 2024 Economic and fiscal outlook (EFO), as spending reviews have approached, governments have increased annual real growth in resource spending over spending review periods by an average 1.1 per cent, equivalent to £6 billion in 2028-29.[footnote 63] Capital spending would need to be an average £2 billion a year higher for the remaining years of the current spending review period to restore its real terms value to that set out in the 2025 Spending Review. These calculations do not include the funding for HMRC and DWP compliance, debt, and fraud and error programs set out in Table 3.2. Including this funding would marginally increase the fall in unprotected departments to 2.7 per cent a year in real terms in the final three years of the forecast.

5.19 There are other longer-term government policy ambitions which would create further pressure on spending beyond the current spending review period but are not yet possible to fully quantify as policy details have not been finalised. These include:

  • the ambition to carry out the biggest council housebuilding programme “since the post-war boom ended in the early 1980s”,[footnote 64] the cost of which would depend on the final details of the programme and its scale. The capital grant required to cover the cost of building a new property for social rent varies between around £150,000 and £200,000 depending on location. The Government expects the existing Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) to deliver 180,000 new social homes between 2026 and 2036.[footnote 65] To illustrate the potential costs of this commitment, we assume that to return council housebuilding to 1980s levels would require at least a further 22,000 houses to be built each year in addition to those expected through the SAHP scheme.[footnote 66] If all these additional houses required capital grants, the additional cost would be between £3 billion and £4 billion each year.

  • As discussed further in Chapter 3, the Government intends to reform social care provision and establish a National Care Service in England. Estimates previously produced by the Health Foundation suggest that, depending on the generosity and design of the system, costs could vary between £3.5 billion and £17 billion a year.[footnote 67]

Welfare spending

5.20 Total welfare spending in the forecast refers to AME spending on social security and tax credits. Around half is subject to the Government’s ‘welfare cap’, which excludes the state pension and those payments most sensitive to the economic cycle (we discuss performance against the cap in Chapter 7). The welfare spending forecast is based on the determinants in the latest economy forecast – principally population, unemployment, earnings, and inflation – and informed by the latest outturn data and Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) models.

5.21 Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19 billion (5.7 per cent) to £353 billion or 11.1 per cent of GDP (Table 5.5). It is then forecast to rise in nominal terms by an average of £16 billion (4.4 per cent) a year over the rest of the forecast period, reaching £431 billion or 11.3 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. This would be 1.3 per cent of GDP higher than its pre-pandemic level of 10.1 per cent of GDP in 2019-20, with 0.5 per cent of GDP of this increase occurring between 2025-26 and 2031-32. Chart 5.6 shows that this rise is driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending, which are forecast to be 0.4 per cent of GDP and 0.3 per cent of GDP higher respectively in 2031-32 than 2025-26, while spending on all other welfare is forecast to fall by 0.2 per cent of GDP over the same period. We explore trends in welfare as a share of GDP further in Box 5.1.

5.22 Health-related benefit caseloads have seen very high rates of growth since the pandemic, with the incapacity caseload growing from 2.5 million to 3.7 million between 2019-20 and 2025-26, and the disability caseload growing from 4.7 million to 6.9 million over the same period.[footnote 68] The extent to which these rates of growth will persist is a highly uncertain component of the forecast. We currently assume that some but not all of the drivers of this growth will persist into the medium term, with health-related spending forecast to grow by an additional 0.4 per cent of GDP over the forecast period on top of the 0.7 per cent of GDP growth observed between 2019-20 and 2025-26. If incapacity and disability caseloads kept increasing at post-pandemic growth rates, spending in 2031-32 would be roughly £25 billion higher than in our central forecast. If growth fell back to pre-pandemic rates, spending in 2031-32 would be roughly £13 billion lower than in our central forecast.

5.23 The latest outturn data on health-related benefit caseloads suggests both downside and upside risks to this judgement. Over the last 18 months, the approval rates at assessment have been falling for both incapacity and child/working-age disability benefits, such that a lower share of new claims receive a benefit award. If this trend were to continue then it could lead to a reduction in future caseloads and expenditure forecasts. Conversely, incapacity off-flow rates have been falling for several years in outturn. If sustained, this could lead to lower off-flows at subsequent forecasts than we are currently expecting, resulting in higher caseloads and expenditure forecasts.

5.24 Relative to the March 2026 forecast, welfare spending is expected to be higher across the forecast by an average of £5 billion a year, and by £6 billion by 2030-31. Table 5.5 shows that this increase is driven by:

  • Higher benefit uprating increases forecast welfare spending by £8 billion in 2030-31. This is mostly driven by higher CPI uprating (£6.1 billion) and higher earnings increasing the triple lock uprating for pensions (£1.5 billion).[footnote 69]

  • Higher forecast health-related universal credit (UC) caseloads increase spending by £3 billion in 2030-31. This is partly driven by the latest outturn data which shows high volumes of new claims for health-related UC in the period since the March forecast.

  • Lower forecast working-age disability benefit onflows decrease spending by £1 billion in 2030-31. New claims for personal independence payment (PIP), the working-age disability benefit, have been higher than expected in 2026, but a much lower proportion of these claims are being awarded the benefit after assessment compared to previous years. The net impact of these two factors reduces the forecast for PIP onflows compared to March.

  • Lower forecast UC fraud and error reduces spending by £2 billion in 2030-31. Following analysis of recent trends in fraud and error in our 2026 Welfare trends report, we have revised down assumptions around the prevalence of fraud and error in UC spending in the forecast period.[footnote 70] The outlook for fraud and error is a particularly uncertain element of the forecast.

5.26 Local authority and HRA borrowing has been at elevated levels since the pandemic, averaging £16 billion a year over the past four years compared to an average of £8 billion in the four years preceding the pandemic. We assume that borrowing levels will not fall significantly from these levels in the near term, but from 2028-29 onwards will fall to an average of £10 billion per year largely reflecting responsibility for funding special educational needs (SEND) provision moving to central government. These judgements are largely unchanged from March 2026, with net borrowing now expected to be an average of £1.5 billion higher each year, across the forecast period. The main components of the local authority and HRA borrowing forecast are:

  • HRAs are the ring-fenced financial accounts used by most LAs in England, Scotland, and Wales to manage the income and spending related to the running of council-owned housing stock. HRA net borrowing has risen strongly in the last decade from £0.2 billion in 2015-16 to a forecast £7 billion this year (see Box 5.2). We forecast HRA net borrowing will decline slightly to £6.4 billion by 2031-32. HRA net borrowing is around £1 billion on average higher than in March, driven by evidence that local authorities have not reduced borrowing in the face of higher interest rates to the degree we previously expected.

  • The cost of SEND deficits is forecast to grow from £3 billion in 2025-26 to £6 billion by 2027-28 as the volume and cost of school-aged children in receipt of EHCPs grows. From 2028-29, all SEND spending will be funded from within central government DEL and so local authorities will no longer have to finance this. The estimated cost of SEND deficits is broadly unchanged from March.

  • Spending enabled by Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)[footnote 71] is forecast to stay broadly flat at around £1 billion over the next five years, following a period in which it increased from £0.3 billion in 2021-22 to £1.4 billion in 2025-26. We previously incorporated a forecast for EFS for only one financial year ahead, but given this sustained rise we now assume it will continue in all years of the forecast.

  • We expect other current spending to be in surplus and reduce overall LA borrowing by an average of £4.6 billion each year, over the forecast period. This reflects our assumption that rising council tax revenues, higher central government grants, the ‘fair funding’ reforms, and central government funding of SEND from 2028-29 strengthens the financial position of LAs over the forecast period.

  • Net capital spending is forecast to fall slightly over the forecast period to £7 billion in 2031-32. We assume that the financial pressures facing local authorities and higher interest rates will lead to lower spending on capital projects, but this is highly uncertain. Relative to March, capital borrowing is higher by around £1 billion on average each year over the forecast period, which reflects local authorities not reducing borrowing in the face of higher interest rates by as much as expected.

5.27 The local authority and HRA forecasts are highly uncertain as they reflect decisions that will be taken by individual local authorities in response to the varied social, economic and financial environments that they face. Financial pressures on local authorities have increased in recent years which is shown by the increased numbers of authorities being granted EFS, from one in 2017-18 to 37 to date in 2026-27. In addition to HRA pressures, discussed in Box 5.2, some of the main pressures and risks in the forecast period include:

  • SEND – local authorities will continue to face financial pressures from SEND related spending until it is fully funded by central government from 2028-29, with local authorities now expecting significantly higher deficits up to 2027-28 compared to their own previous estimates.[footnote 72] There is uncertainty around the impact that the recent reforms in February 2026 will have on costs and on the numbers of children that receive support. Further, while the Government has committed to reimburse local authorities for 90 per cent of the deficits they accumulated on SEND spending through to the end of 2025-26,[footnote 73] the Government has made no commitment in relation to deficits accumulated after that point.

  • Temporary accommodation and asylum – English local authority spending on housing support outside of the HRA has grown from £2 billion in 2010-11 to £4 billion in 2025-26, driven by increases in the cost of provision of housing for homeless families and for refugees transitioning out of asylum accommodation. The Government’s ambitions to reduce the level of homelessness and improve the standard of temporary accommodation are likely to increase pressure on local authority spending in this area.

  • Social care – which in 2025-26 accounted for around 30 per cent of local government current expenditure in England – £44 billion – compared with around 20 per cent in 2010-11. Adult social care costs are likely to increase further given the ageing population, rising demand among working-age adults, inflation and the minimum wage. Local authorities in England also spent around £17 billion on social care for children in 2025-26 and the number of children in England looked after by local authorities grew from 64,000 in 2010 to 82,000 in 2025.[footnote 74]

Box 5.2: The financial position of local authority Housing Revenue Accounts

Housing Revenue Accounts (HRAs) are the financial accounts that the majority of local authorities use for the management, maintenance and improvement of around 2 million council homes in England, Scotland and Wales, which is around 7 per cent of the total stock of homes. Over the past decade, the financial position of many HRAs has come under increasing pressure. This reflects constrained rental income growth and rising expenditure costs.

Rental income accounts for around 90 per cent of HRA income and is largely determined by government policy on social rents and the stock of housing. The stock of council housing in England has declined from over 5 million in 1980 to 1.6 million today, largely due to houses purchased under Right to Buy and some large-scale voluntary transfers of homes to private registered housing providers. In parallel, rents have largely not kept up with the rate of inflation in the last decade. Between the late 2000s and mid-2010s, social housing landlords, including local authorities, were generally permitted to increase rents by inflation plus an additional uplift. Policy reform in the 2015 Summer Budget required social rents in England to fall by 1 per cent a year between 2016-17 and 2019-20. Thereafter, rent increases resumed but remained subject to government regulation and have often been capped below prevailing inflation rates. Earlier this year, the government introduced a 10-year settlement from April 2026 to allow social housing landlords to increase rents by CPI+1 percentage point annually.

The cost of construction and maintenance in the housing sector has increased substantially over the past decade, growing by over 40 per cent.a The impact of this is illustrated in the right panel of Chart A, which shows that the total costs of HRA capital works has risen even while the volume of works has fallen. Following the Grenfell Tower fire and subsequent reforms to social housing regulation, social landlords, including councils, have faced further spending pressure to meet the growing obligations to improve the quality and safety of housing, while also meeting separate obligations to improve the energy efficiency of the housing stock.

As a result of these trends, as shown in the left panel of Chart C, the HRA net borrowing position has increased from around £0.1 billion to over £6 billion in the last decade. This reflects that HRA capital expenditure has increased from £5 billion in 2014-15 to £10 billion in 2024-25, and total spending has risen from £10 billion to £18 billion, while in the same period income has only increased from £10 billion to £12 billion.

Debt interest spending

5.28 Debt interest spending as a share of GDP is forecast to rise from 3.9 per cent of GDP in 2026-27 to reach 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2031-32 (Chart 5.7). This would be above the previous highs reached in the 1960s and 1980s and more than double the average of the ten years prior to the pandemic. The increase in debt interest costs since the pandemic has been driven by both the rising stock of debt and by the sharp increases in interest rates over that period. However, interest rates are not high by historical standards, as is also shown in Chart 5.7. The effective interest rate[footnote 75] on government debt of around 4 per cent over the forecast period is less than half the 1980s peak, of 10 per cent, and below the average rate over the two decades preceding the 2008 financial crisis of 7.5 per cent.

5.29 In nominal terms, debt interest spending is forecast to rise from £124 billion in 2026-27 to £160 billion in 2031-32, an average year-on-year increase of around £7 billion. This is driven by new borrowing which increases the stock of debt on which interest accrues each year. In addition, an average of £184 billion of maturing gilts are refinanced each year, typically at higher interest rates than the debt they replaced, which also contributes to the rise in spending. In 2030-31, the year-on-year increase in debt interest spending slows to £2.2 billion because the alignment of RPI with CPIH[footnote 76] reduces RPI growth and therefore the uplift applied to index-linked gilts. In the final year of the forecast, year-on-year growth in debt interest spending returns to the previous trend, increasing by £10 billion, reflecting new borrowing and significant redemptions in that year from the large volume of gilts issued during the Covid period. Chapter 6 has further discussion of the impact of redemptions and the change in the maturity composition of gilt issuance.

5.30 Compared to March, debt interest is forecast to be £14 billion higher on average over the forecast period. This largely reflects higher RPI inflation in the near term and higher Bank Rate and gilt rates expectations in the medium term:

  • Revisions to the RPI inflation forecast increase spending by £12 billion in 2026-27 and £6.5 billion in 2027-28, and then by an average of £1.2 billion until 2030-31.

  • Higher Bank Rate and gilt rates are forecast to increase debt interest costs compared to March 2026 by £3.9 billion in 2026-27 and then by an average of £11 billion a year throughout the forecast period.

  • Financing and other factors are expected to decrease spending in the first two years of the forecast, by an average of £0.9 billion, but then increase it by £0.8 billion in 2030-31.

  • The effects of policy decrease debt interest in 2026-27 by £0.9 billion, which reflects the direct impact on inflation of policy measures this year, and then raises it by an average of £0.8 billion a year thereafter mostly due to increased borrowing.

PSNB-neutral spending and other annually managed expenditure

5.31 PSNB-neutral spending includes spending which is offset in receipts and therefore does not affect public sector net borrowing (PSNB). PSNB-neutral spending has increased by £0.9 billion on average since the March 2026 forecast. The main changes are increases in depreciation and VAT refunds, and decreases in environmental levies, which are described in paragraphs 4.46-4.51 of Chapter 4.

5.32 Some of the main other items of AME spending include:

  • Net spending on unfunded public service pensions is forecast to move from a deficit of £1.1 billion in 2026-27 to a deficit of £14 billion in 2027-28. This is primarily due to the 2024 valuation of these schemes, described in more detail in paragraph 5.8, which reduces employer contributions and increases net pension spending by around £16 billion a year from 2027-28 onwards. The lower employer contributions represent a saving for departments, which are offset by a broadly equivalent reduction in RDEL, leaving overall spending around £1.1 billion higher a year. Spending is also around £2 billion higher than in March due to higher forecast inflation and pensioner caseloads. From 2027-28, the deficit is expected to remain largely flat in cash terms at around £15 billion and therefore to fall slightly as a share of GDP.

  • Public corporations excluding the HRA are forecast to spend £8 billion on capital by 2030-31, around £1 billion more than we forecast in March 2026. This is driven by a combination of new outturn data which was around £0.6 billion higher than expected in March and changes to the nominal GDP forecast.

  • The cost of the Post Office redress and Infected Blood compensation schemes is expected to peak at £3.8 billion in 2026-27 before falling to £0.2 billion in 2031-32.[footnote 77] Spending on these schemes was £1.5 billion less in 2025-26 than expected in the March 2026. Given the ongoing rollout of these schemes, there remains uncertainty around the number of eligible claimants, average award amounts and how quickly claims will be processed which could change the total amount of spending and its profile.

  • Capital spending on the construction of the Sizewell C nuclear power station, which is estimated to be £3.7 billion in 2026-27 before rising slightly to £3.9 billion in 2031-32. Compared to the March 2026 forecast, spending is expected to be an average of £0.8 billion higher between 2026-27 and 2029-30 reflecting Sizewell C’s revised plan to frontload more of the total capital spending.

Chapter 6: Fiscal aggregates

Introduction

6.1 This chapter details how changes in our pre-measures forecast, and policy measures since our March 2026 forecast, affect key summary measures of the public finances, including:

  • deficit aggregates, including public sector net borrowing (PSNB), the difference between expenditure and receipts; the current budget deficit, the difference between current (day-to-day) expenditure and receipts; the primary deficit, the difference between non-interest expenditure and receipts; and cyclically adjusted measures of the deficit, which take account of the position of the economy relative to its potential level of output;

  • financial transactions, which capture the effects of public sector net lending, sales or purchases of financial assets, and interventions which affect the Bank of England’s (BoE’s) balance sheet; and

  • balance sheet aggregates, including public sector net debt (PSND), which includes all debt obligations net of liquid financial assets; public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL), which includes all financial liabilities and financial assets; and public sector net worth (PSNW), which includes all financial and non-financial assets and liabilities.

Deficit aggregates

Borrowing and the current budget deficit

6.2 Chart 6.1 shows that public sector net borrowing increased sharply to 10.2 per cent of GDP in 2009-10 following the financial crisis, before falling in each subsequent year to reach 2.0 per cent of GDP in 2018-19. It then increased again to a record high of 14.7 per cent of GDP in 2020-21 due to the pandemic and the policy response to it, reflecting both the large rise in cash borrowing and the fall in nominal GDP in that year. After the pandemic, borrowing fell to around 5 per cent of GDP in 2021-22 and remained close to that level for the following three years before falling again to 4.4 per cent in 2025-26.

6.3 Chart 6.1 and Table 6.1 show that, in our central forecast, PSNB is expected to fall slightly from 4.4 per cent of GDP (£134 billion) in 2025-26 to 4.2 per cent (£133 billion) in 2026-27. It then declines steadily to reach 1.8 per cent of GDP (£67 billion) in 2030-31 and remains flat as a share of GDP in 2031-32. PSNB is now expected to be higher in each year of the forecast compared to March, by 0.5 per cent of GDP in the near term and 0.2 per cent of GDP in 2030-31.

6.4 Chart 6.1 and Table 6.1 also show that the current budget deficit is forecast to fall from 1.5 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 (£47 billion) to 1.3 per cent (£41 billion) in 2026-27. It is then forecast to improve in each year to reach a surplus of 0.4 per cent of GDP (£15 billion) in 2029-30, rising to 0.6 per cent in 2030-31 (£22 billion) but then falling to 0.5 per cent (£21 billion) in 2031-32. As with PSNB, the forecast for the current budget deficit has seen a moderate deterioration in each year compared to the March.

6.6 Both PSNB and the current budget deficit are expected to fall gradually as a share of GDP over the forecast, but these improvements begin to level off by the end of the forecast period, with PSNB remaining flat and the current budget deficit declining slightly as a share of GDP in 2031-32. Box 6.1: The forecast rise in underlying borrowing from 2030-31 to 2031-32

In the central pre-measures forecast, that is before accounting for the effects of new policy measures, public sector net borrowing falls year on year by around half a per cent of GDP until 2030-31, at which point it is forecast to rise by 0.1 per cent to 2.0 per cent of GDP (Table A). This is an unusual pattern because typically at the end of the forecast – when the economy is usually assumed to be growing at trend and departmental spending is often assumed to be rising in line with nominal GDP – borrowing would be expected to be falling as a share of GDP. This is often driven by ‘fiscal drag’, where tax receipts rise as a share of GDP because earnings are assumed to rise faster than CPI inflation (which is used to uprate personal tax thresholds at the end of the forecast) and by some other areas of underlying buoyancy in the tax regime.

In the current forecast, however, public sector current receipts increase by an average of 0.3 per cent of GDP a year between 2026-27 and 2030-31, but are then flat at 42.6 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. Total managed expenditure falls between 2026-27 and 2030-31, by an average of 0.2 per cent of GDP, but then rises slightly in the final year. So the rise in PSNB in 2031-32 in the pre-measures forecast is driven by flat receipts and slightly rising spending as shares of GDP.

The drivers of these trends relate to the emergence of pressures that we identified in the 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability (FRS) report and which will intensify over the longer term. Specifically, the upward pressure on pension spending from the ageing population, the reduction in tax revenues from the loss of fuel duty due to the transition to electric vehicles, and the increasing cost of debt interest due to the rising stock of debt. Looking at these components in more detail:

  • Welfare spending is forecast to rise by around 0.1 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. This reflects increasing health-related caseloads and forecast growth in the state pension caseload due to the ageing population. Over previous years of the forecast, the underlying upward trend in pensioner spending is suppressed by the increase to the state pension age between April 2026 and March 2028. This is assessed in more detail in Box 5.1.

  • Fuel duty receipts are forecast to decline slightly as a share of GDP in 2031-32, as the loss of revenue due to the transition to electric vehicles is greater than the increase in revenue from the assumed increase in fuel duty rates at this point. In addition, there are small declines in revenue as a share of GDP from assumed declines in the consumption of tobacco and alcohol, and from declining oil and gas revenues, as discussed in Chapter 4. Overall, the decline in revenues from these sources push up on borrowing by around 0.1 per cent of GDP.

  • Debt interest spending increases borrowing by a further 0.1 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. This is driven by the rising stock of debt and by the rising number of gilts that are forecast to be refinanced at this time horizon at higher interest rates, discussed further in paragraph 5.29.

Overall, in 2031-32, these three effects increase borrowing by around 0.3 per cent of GDP, which more than offsets all the other pre-measures year-on-year changes to tax and spending which are forecast to reduce borrowing in 2031-32 by around 0.2 per cent of GDP. This includes some fiscal drag as earnings are forecast to rise faster than CPI at this time horizon. However, this effect is more muted than in previous years of the forecast where the personal tax thresholds are frozen.

In this Budget, the Government has decided to reduce the pre-measures assumption for the growth in departmental spending in 2031-32, which, combined with policies to increase taxation, helps reduce the forecast for borrowing in this year by 0.2 per cent of GDP. This means that, after the impact of policy, borrowing remains flat between 2030-31 and 2031-32 as a share of GDP. This is an early indication of the additional pressures that the long-term trends highlighted in the 2026 FRS will create for policy-makers aiming to put the public finances on a sustainable path over the coming decades.

This primarily reflects higher debt interest spending, due to higher RPI inflation and interest rates, which increase borrowing by an average of £14 billion each year.   • Upwards revisions to the pre-measures receipts forecast which reduce PSNB by an average of £17 billion per year.   • The direct effect of Budget policy measures, which increase PSNB in each year until 2028-29, reflecting policy decisions which reduce receipts in 2026-27 and increase spending in each year. Other deficit measures

6.11 Other deficit measures also provide relevant information on the state of the public finances. The primary deficit, which excludes net interest spending, is a useful proxy of the extent to which discretionary spending is covered by revenues. All measures of the deficit can be presented in cyclically adjusted terms, correcting for an estimate of the position in the economic cycle, which provides a rough indication of the underlying or structural deficit:

  • The primary deficit moves from 1 per cent of GDP this year to a surplus of 1.7 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. If achieved, this would be the largest primary surplus since 2000-01. Compared to the March forecast the primary deficit is an average of 0.1 per cent of GDP higher in each year until 2029-30, but the same in 2030-31. This reflects that the medium-term deterioration in PSNB compared to March can be seen as driven largely by higher net interest spending, with other changes to spending and receipts broadly offsetting.

  • Cyclically adjusted measures of the deficit are 0.7 per cent of GDP below the unadjusted metrics in 2026-27 and 2027-28. The gap narrows over each of the subsequent years until 2031-32 when it closes. This reflects the negative output gap this year and subsequent closing of the output gap across the forecast.

Financial transactions

6.12 Changes in public sector net debt and wider balance sheet aggregates, including public sector net financial liabilities, are calculated by combining changes in borrowing with changes in financial transactions and valuation effects. Financial transactions capture the effects of public sector net lending, sales or purchases of financial assets, and interventions which affect the Bank of England’s (BoE’s) balance sheet. They also convert the accrued measures of tax and spending which underpin our forecast for borrowing into the cash flows relevant to debt. Valuation effects capture changes in the value of the assets or liabilities held by the public sector which count toward the measure of net debt.

6.13 In nominal terms public sector net debt is forecast to increase in each year from 2026-27 onwards, by an average of £129 billion a year. Table 6.3 breaks down the contribution to the year-on-year increases in PSND from public sector net borrowing, pre-measures financial transactions, policy measures which affect financial transactions, and valuation effects. It shows:

  • Public sector net borrowing is forecast to increase PSND in each year from 2026-27, by an average of £92 billion, as discussed in paragraph 6.7.

  • Pre-measures financial transactions increase debt in each year of the forecast, due to:

  • The cost of student loans, which increase debt on average £9 billion a year over the forecast reflecting new lending to students.

    • Repayments to the Bank of England’s Term Funding Scheme (TFS) which reduce debt by £26 billion in 2026-27. The TFS then has no further effect until 2030-31 where it reduces debt by £16 billion due to the expected one-off payment as the scheme comes to an end.

    • Losses on gilts held within the Asset Purchase Facility (APF), incurred when gilts are sold for less than their face value, raise debt by an average of £4.3 billion a year.

    • Net lending and purchases of equity by public financial institutions (PuFins) increase debt by an average of £3.1 billion each year.[footnote 78]

  • Cash flow timing effects, which convert the accrued measures of tax and spending in the forecast for borrowing into the cash flows relevant to debt, raise debt by an average of £19 billion a year. Of this, accruals adjustments for taxes contribute an average of £10 billion a year and the removal of modified interest on student loans an average of £9 billion a year.

  • The direct effects of policy measures on financial transactions increase debt in every year of the forecast, apart from 2029-30, by on average of £2.7 billion. This is mainly due to policies which increase the funding for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to invest in financial assets (see paragraph 3.20 for more detail). In 2029-30, the policy to introduce timely payment for self assessment decreases debt by £17 billion due to the additional tax payments brought forward to that year (see paragraph 3.13 for more detail). These cash payments have no effect on accrued measures such as PSNB or PSNFL.

  • Valuation effects increase debt by £11 billion in 2026-27 and an average of £1.2 billion thereafter. These largely reflect the consequences of new gilts being issued at a discount to the face value they are recorded at in the public finances, an effect which subsides over the forecast as we assume that a greater proportion of gilts are issued for nearer to face value.

Financing requirement

6.19 Public sector net borrowing is comprised of central government, local government, and public corporations’ borrowing. The central government net cash requirement (CGNCR), which only covers central government and is on a cash basis, forms the basis of the Debt Management Office’s (DMO’s) financing remit and so is the primary driver of the net issuance of gilts.

6.20 Table 6.6 shows the relationship between the CGNCR and PSNB. First, financial transactions are added to borrowing to get the cash requirement of the whole public sector (PSNCR). The cash requirements for non-central government (local authorities, public corporations and Network Rail) are then removed to get to the CGNCR excluding Network Rail (CGNCR ex), which is the measure that feeds directly into the Government’s gilt issuance plans, which also cover the rolling over of maturing debt securities.

6.21 The CGNCR ex is forecast to be £144 billion this year, to peak at £150 billion in 2028-29, and then to fall to £105 billion at the end of the forecast. It is on average £36 billion higher per year than PSNB across the forecast period, which largely reflects the additional financing required for the financial transactions set out in paragraph 6.13. Changes since the March forecast are broadly similar to changes in PSNB in 2028-29 and 2030-31. In 2026-27 and 2027-28, the change in CGNCR ex compared to March is considerably less than the change in PSNB. This is because the inflation driven increases to the cost of index-linked gilts only affects the accrued measures of borrowing and does not need to be financed for many years. In 2029-30, the £17 billion of additional cash payments associated with the policy to introduce timely payment for self assessment (explained in further detail in paragraph 3.13) reduces the CGNCR ex, but does not affect PSNB.

6.23 More generally, the composition of gilts issued by the DMO in recent years has become skewed toward shorter maturities. As interest rates are lower at shorter maturities this has decreased interest costs for the Government in the near term. However, it increases the value of gilts that are redeemed and require refinancing in future, so increasing sensitivity to changes in rates. Box 6.2: The trajectories of PSND and PSND excluding the Bank of England

Public sector net debt (PSND) is the stock of the public sector’s gross debt liabilities minus its liquid financial assets. In 2016, the ONS also produced a new measure of public sector net debt excluding the Bank of England (PSND ex BoE), which excludes assets and liabilities on the Bank of England’s balance sheet, with a historical series extending back to April 1997. Material differences between the two measures emerged in the 2010s, due to:

  • The Bank’s quantitative easing (QE) programme introduced in 2009. The creation of central bank reserves to purchase assets for QE, held in the Asset Purchase Facility (APF), initially increased PSND as the reserve liabilities came to have a higher value than the assets.a

  • The Term Funding Scheme (TFS), which was introduced by the Bank in 2016 to support bank lending. The loan assets held by the TFS are not counted as liquid assets in PSND, while the reserves created by the Bank for this scheme are liabilities that increase PSND.

These schemes therefore initially increased PSND and not PSND ex BoE. As Chart A shows, this led to a divergence between the two measures which widened as the schemes expanded over the 2010s and early 2020s, with the gap reaching 13.1 per cent of GDP in 2021-22. Subsequently the gap has narrowed as the APF has been unwound and loans on the TFS repaid to reach 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2025-26. We assume this will continue over the forecast period with the gap expected to narrow to 1.6 per cent of GDP in 2031-32. This means that, between 2021-22 and 2025-26, PSND fell marginally as a share of GDP because the unwind of the APF and TFS more than offset the upward pressure on debt from high levels of government borrowing. By contrast, PSND ex BoE rose steadily over this period, though from a lower level, because the APF and TFS effects are excluded. PSND ex BoE therefore provides a better picture of the underlying trajectory of the fiscal position driven by government borrowing over this period.

Public sector net financial liabilities

6.27 Public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL) is the balance sheet measure that is targeted in the Government’s fiscal rules. It includes non-debt liabilities such as funded pensions, and additional illiquid financial assets such as loans (most notably student loans) and equity (including the assets of funded pension schemes). In nominal terms, from a stock of £2.6 trillion in 2025-26, PSNFL is forecast to increase by £133 billion in 2026-27, £83 billion in 2029-30 and by smaller amounts in the following two years. Table 6.7 shows the year-on-year changes in PSNFL are mainly driven by PSNB, as well as:

  • Valuation changes in funded pension schemes, which reduce PSNFL in 2026-27 by £8 billion, but increase it thereafter. This reflects a judgement that equity assets held within the schemes will increase in value faster than the pension liabilities in 2026-27, but that this effect reverses over the remainder of the forecast.

  • Asset Purchase Facility sales losses, incurred when gilts are sold for less than their redemption value. These add to PSNFL by amounts rising year on year until 2029-30 and around £5 billion by 2031-32.

  • The discount on new issuance of central government gilts (gilt premia) pushes up PSNFL by £8 billion in 2026-27 and £2.6 billion in 2027-28. This effect subsides, with smaller increases of £0.9 billion a year on average thereafter, as gilt prices rise and new debt is assumed to issued nearer to face value.

  • Increases in the value of general government equity assets. These capture growth in public sector equity assets not held in funded pension schemes and include the equity holdings of PuFins. They reduce PSNFL by an average of £4.2 billion a year.

  • Reserves and other valuation changes, which increase PSNFL by £2.5 billion in 2026-27 largely due to a reduction in the value of the UK’s foreign reserve assets. They have little effect thereafter as we assume a constant exchange rate.

Public sector net worth

6.29 Public sector net worth (PSNW) is the broadest measure of the Government’s balance sheet, capturing changes in the value of non-financial assets (NFAs) and the liabilities associated with unfunded pension schemes, in addition to what is included in PSNFL. Inverted PSNW falls by 3.5 per cent of GDP from 63.3 per cent in 2026-27 to 59.8 per cent in 2031-32, driven by a 1.9 per cent of GDP rise in the value of NFAs. Compared to our March forecast, inverted PSNW is 0.3 per cent of GDP lower in 2026-27, largely due to lower-than-forecast outturn for 2025-26. This difference gradually reverses, leaving it 1.4 per cent of GDP higher by 2030-31, reflecting the upwards revisions to our forecast for PSNFL, in combination with faster forecast growth in unfunded pensions liabilities.
