6.31 Box 6.3 discusses the impact of the possible reclassification of water companies for the public sector balance sheets measures and for borrowing and the current budget deficit.

Box 6.3: Potential impact of water companies on the public finances

Water companies in England and Wales have been classified within the private sector since 1989. The Office for National Statistics (ONS), however, is currently reviewing this classification in response to the Water (Special Measures) Act 2025, which increased the degree of government control over the operation of water companies.a,b The Government has also recently announced its intention to further increase public control of the industry, including by removing caps on government share ownership in water firms.c If the ONS were to reclassify, then the relevant assets, liabilities, revenue and expenditure of providers would be incorporated to the public sector.

The 2025 Fiscal risks and sustainability report assessed the potential impact of reclassifying the full water sector on the public sector balance sheet in 2023-24, showing that this could:

  • Increase gross liabilities, which increase PSNFL, by £91 billion (3.3 per cent of GDP), including £66 billion of debt. Borrowing by water companies has increased in recent years with around half (52 per cent) of debt inflation-linked.

  • Increase financial assets, which all reduce PSNFL, by £12 billion (0.4 per cent of GDP). This includes £5 billion in cash held by water companies, the only financial assets which would reduce PSND.

  • Overall, increase PSNFL by £78 billion (2.8 per cent of GDP). PSNW, as the widest measure of the balance sheet, would additionally include the £94 billion of water companies’ physical assets, including water pipelines, treatment facilities, and reservoirs which account for 88 per cent of their total assets.

This increase in PSNFL would be incorporated as a one-off increase to its level at the point of reclassification. Following the initial increase in the level of PSNFL, only the level of borrowing by water companies would directly affect the trajectory of PSNFL, and so affect the Government’s supplementary fiscal target which is for PSNFL to be declining as a share of GDP in the third year of the forecast.

Table B illustrates the potential impact of reclassification on the level of borrowing and the current budget deficit if the revenue and expenditure of providers were to be moved into the public sector, by using data from the outturn years between 2020-21 and 2024-25.d,e Within these years, we estimate that reclassification could:

  • Increase public sector receipts by £13 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) a year on average. Within this, revenue from consumer bills averaged £12 billion and interest receipts averaged £0.4 billion a year.

  • Increase current spending by £11 billion (0.4 per cent of GDP) a year. Within this, operating costs, mainly comprising of wages and contracted services, averaged £7 billion, and dividend and debt interest payments averaged £3.8 billion.

  • Increase capital spending by £6 billion (0.2 per cent of GDP) a year. Most investment by water companies is on capital additions of property, plant and equipment.

  • Increase the current budget deficit, in most years, by £1.0 billion a year (less than 0.1 per cent of GDP). This is because, in outturn, current spending and depreciation is largely offset by receipts, and most borrowing by water companies is to fund investment.

  • Increase net borrowing by £4.4 billion (0.2 per cent of GDP) a year. The increase in borrowing rises from £0.2 billion in 2020-21 to £7 billion by 2024-25. This is because both capital and current spending have increased by more than receipts over this period.

Chapter 7: Fiscal context, targets and uncertainty

Introduction

7.1 In this chapter, we assess the Government’s performance against its fiscal rules alongside a wider analysis of fiscal sustainability. This includes an examination of the fiscal context, the main risks to the fiscal outlook, and long-term fiscal pressures. As such, in this chapter we:

  • assess the fiscal context for this Budget, by summarising changes in public sector net borrowing and public sector net debt in the post-war period, comparing the UK fiscal position to that of other advanced economies, and assessing the outlook for longer-term fiscal sustainability in the UK;

  • set out the Government’s fiscal targets and estimate their likelihood of being met under current policy conditions in our central forecast, and assess the fiscal position against wider metrics for fiscal sustainability; and

  • examine key risks and uncertainties around the central forecast using analysis based on: an assessment of specific risks to the central forecast; patterns of shocks to, and variations in, key macroeconomic and fiscal determinants; and analysis of the impact on the fiscal forecast of alternative economic scenarios.

The fiscal context

Current and historical fiscal position

7.2 The left panel of Chart 7.1 shows that over the past two decades, public sector net borrowing (PSNB) as a share of GDP has, on average, been markedly higher than over the preceding 60 years. Borrowing has averaged 5.8 per cent of GDP in the period since the global financial crisis (5.3 per cent of GDP excluding the pandemic-hit year of 2020-21), three times the post-war average of 1.9 per cent of GDP in the period up until 2008.

7.3 Following the Covid pandemic, borrowing remained at around 5 per cent of GDP for four years until 2024-25. In the following two years, it has fallen and is now forecast to reach 4.2 per cent of GDP in 2026-27. In the latest central forecast, under the government’s planned fiscal consolidation, borrowing is expected to fall further to 1.8 per cent of GDP by 2031-32, which, if achieved, would be broadly in line with the post-war, pre-2008 average. The right panel of Chart 7.1 shows that in successive forecasts since the pandemic, governments have typically planned to reduce borrowing to the pre-2008 average of below 2 per cent of GDP. However, in practice over the period since then, there has so far only been a slight decline in borrowing in outturn years to 4.4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26. This has been as a result of the fiscal impact of subsequent economic shocks, weaker-than-expected growth, and discretionary policy decisions to delay consolidation.

7.4 The left panel of Chart 7.2 shows changes in public sector net debt, excluding the Bank of England (PSND ex BoE), also referred to as underlying debt, as a share of GDP since 1948-49. The three decades following the Second World War saw a steady fall from the very high debt level of around 250 per cent of GDP reached immediately after the war. This fall was supported by high real economic growth and a substantial fall in defence spending. From the late 1970s, debt broadly stabilised between 20 and 40 per cent of GDP, and stood at around 36 per cent on the eve of the financial crisis in 2007-08.

7.5 The fiscal impact of the financial crisis led underlying debt to rise sharply to reach a peak of 79 per cent in 2014-15 before then falling slightly in the late 2010s. It then once again rose markedly due to the impact of the pandemic to reach 86 per cent in 2020-21. Following the pandemic, after an initial decline, underlying debt has continued to rise in all years, due to the relatively elevated level of borrowing in this period described above, to reach 92 per cent of GDP in 2026-27. This would be 57 percentage points of GDP higher than the pre-financial-crisis level.

7.6 The right panel of Chart 7.2 compares the forecast changes in underlying debt over the post-pandemic period relative to actual outturn. Successive previous forecasts have expected debt to fall or stabilise over the medium term. In practice, this has yet to occur for the same reasons that the recent forecasts for falling borrowing, described above, have not yet been delivered. In the latest forecast, PSND ex BoE is projected to peak in 2028-29 at 95 per cent of GDP and then subsequently fall slightly. If this were to be achieved, it would still leave the level of debt 7 percentage points of GDP higher in 2031-32 than the November 2022 forecast peak; 5 percentage points higher than the 2025-26 figure of 89 per cent of GDP; and at elevated levels compared to the past 50 years.

International context

7.7 As discussed above, unexpected shocks and low growth have contributed to elevated levels of borrowing and significant increases in public debt in the last two decades. While these factors have affected nearly all advanced economies, the UK has experienced a more significant deterioration in the public finances than most. The left side of Chart 7.3 shows that while general government net borrowing in the UK (blue line) has followed a similar overall trend to other G7 (purple line) and advanced (yellow line) economies since 2006, it has consistently been at a higher level and saw larger spikes in response to shocks. Between 2022 and 2026, UK net borrowing on an internationally comparable basis was 5.1 per cent of GDP, 1.3 percentage points higher than the average for other G7 economies and 3.8 percentage points higher than the average for other advanced economies.

7.8 Based on the IMF forecasts shown in these charts, borrowing in the UK is expected by the IMF to decline by 2.4 per cent of GDP to 1.4 per cent in 2031 – which would be close to the IMF’s forecasts for the average for other advanced economies.[footnote 85] As described in paragraph 7.3, recent similar plans have subsequently been delayed due to economic shocks, weaker-than-expected growth, and changes to government policy.

7.9 The right panel of Chart 7.3 shows that the higher borrowing in the UK than in comparable economies over the previous two decades has contributed to a larger increase in its debt stock over time. General government net debt in the UK as a share of GDP (on an internationally comparable basis) has gone from 8 percentage points higher than the average for other advanced economies in 2006 to 53 percentage points higher in 2026. Over this period among G7 economies, the UK has experienced the largest increase in net debt as a share of GDP, increasing from 25 percentage points below the average of other G7 economies in 2006 to 6 percentage points higher in 2026. Even with the fiscal consolidation planned over the forecast period, the IMF expects UK general government net debt to decline only marginally between 2026 and 2031, to end broadly level with the IMF’s forecasts for the average of other G7 economies, and 54 percentage points higher than its level in 2006.

Long-term sustainability of the public finances

7.10 In the 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, we explored the major sources of long-term fiscal pressure and set out projections for the public finances over the next 50 years. In nearly all of the long-term scenarios we produced, including under several different assumptions for long-term policy settings, demographic and other cost pressures were projected to eventually move borrowing and debt onto an ever-rising trajectory. The blue line in Chart 7.4 shows how the upward trajectory of debt in the FRS baseline long-term scenario starts to accelerate onto an unsustainable path in the 2040s.

7.11 The baseline long-term scenario shown in Chart 7.4 took, as its starting point, the March 2026 forecast for a fiscal consolidation in which the primary balance moves from a deficit of 1.4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to a surplus of 1.5 per cent of GDP in 2030-31. However, Chart 7.1 showed that successive recent plans for fiscal consolidation have not yet been delivered. If the long-term projections were instead based on the primary deficit in 2030-31 remaining at its 2025-26 level, the yellow line shows that debt is projected to start to rise onto an unsustainable upward trajectory in the early 2030s. This highlights the importance of early policy action to keep debt on a sustainable trajectory.

7.12 Some of the pressures which drive the increase in debt in the FRS long-term scenarios, such as the impact of an ageing population on state pension caseloads and declining tax revenue from emissions-related taxes, are already starting to affect the fiscal position over the medium term. Box 6.1 explains how some of these factors contribute to the increase in borrowing in the pre-measures forecast between 2030-31 and 2031-32, underlining the importance of early action to address these pressures.

7.13 The Government’s decision to replace the state pension triple lock with an adjusted triple lock from April 2030 should, in itself, reduce some of the long-term upward pressure on the public finances that was identified in the 2026 FRS. Provisional analysis suggests that, if the next 50 years are similar to the previous 35 years, the adjusted triple lock could reduce the projected increase in debt by around 25 per cent of GDP in 2075-76 relative to the current triple lock uprating. However, alongside this announcement the Government also set out an ambition to expand public provision of social care. The overall impact of these announcements on the outlook for long-term fiscal sustainability therefore depends on the costs of the reforms to social care. These issues are discussed further in paragraphs 3.48 to 3.54.

Fiscal targets and wider indicators of fiscal sustainability

7.14 The Budget Responsibility and National Audit Act 2011 requires the OBR to assess at least once per financial year the extent to which the Government has achieved or is likely to achieve its fiscal mandate under current policy. The Charter for Budget Responsibility states that the fiscal mandate is:

  • to have the current budget in surplus in 2029-30, until 2029-30 becomes the third year of the forecast period. From that point, the current budget must then remain in balance or in surplus from the third year of the rolling forecast periods.

7.15 There are also two supplementary targets in the Charter:

  • to have debt, defined as public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL), falling as a share of the economy in 2029-30, until 2029-30 becomes the third year of the forecast period. Debt should then fall by the third year of the rolling forecast period; and

  • to ensure that expenditure on welfare (excluding the state pension and payments closely linked to the economic cycle) is contained within a predetermined cap and margin. The Charter sets out that the OBR will assess spending against the welfare cap and margin at the first Budget of each new Parliament.

7.16 The Charter also requires the OBR to provide an analysis of the risks surrounding the fiscal outlook, and to consider a wide range of factors and dimensions relating to the sustainability of the public finances. The Charter further states that the Treasury will consider a wide range of indicators in its management of fiscal policy.

Performance against the Government’s fiscal targets in the central forecast

7.17 Based on the central forecast and as shown in Table 7.1, the centres of the distribution of forecast outcomes for the current budget and the PSNFL-to-GDP ratio are such that:

  • The fiscal mandate for the current budget to be in surplus in 2029-30, the third year of the forecast period, is met by a margin of 0.4 per cent of GDP (£15 billion). This compares to a margin of 0.6 per cent of GDP (£22 billion) when performance against the rules was last assessed alongside the November 2025 Budget.

  • The supplementary target, for public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL) to be falling as a per cent of GDP in 2029-30, is forecast to be met by a margin of 0.7 per cent of GDP (£24 billion), unchanged from a margin of 0.7 per cent of GDP (also £24 billion) at the November 2025 Budget.

  • The welfare cap plus margin, set for 2029-30, is on course to not be met by a margin of £3 billion, as opposed to last November when it was forecast to be met by a margin of £2 billion.

Probability of meeting the fiscal targets

7.18 Chart 7.5 presents fan charts, based on stochastic simulations and historic deviations from central forecasts, of the probability distribution around the forecast for the current budget and PSNFL.[footnote 86] These distributions enable us to assess the probability of the Government’s fiscal targets being met based on current policies. They show that currently:

  • The probability of meeting the fiscal mandate to have the current budget in surplus in 2029-30 is now 56 per cent in the post-measures forecast. This is a slight reduction from last November’s 59 per cent. With the shorter horizon to the target year compared to last November, a smaller margin is required to have the same chance of meeting the rules. Despite this, the probability has decreased overall because the reduction in the margin more than offsets the effect of the shorter horizon. For the probability of meeting the fiscal mandate to be increased to reach 60 or 70 per cent, it would require the current budget forecast to be in surplus by around £25 and £50 billion, respectively, in 2029-30, instead of the current forecast margin of £15 billion.

  • The probability of meeting the supplementary target, PSNFL falling as a share of GDP, is now 54 per cent. The estimated likelihood has increased slightly from 52 per cent in November 2025, primarily due to a reduction in the uncertainty around the central forecast for the target year having rolled forward from the fourth to the third year of the forecast. For the probability of the supplementary target to be met by a 60 or 70 per cent chance, it would require PSNFL to be falling by 1.8 or 3.9 per cent of GDP in 2029-30, respectively, instead of the current forecast margin of a fall of 0.7 per cent of GDP.

7.19 Chart 7.5 illustrates the very wide range of possible outcomes around the central forecast for the current deficit and PSNFL. In this forecast, the probability distribution suggests that there is a 60 per cent chance that the current budget deficit falls between a deficit of 2.0 per cent of GDP (around £70 billion) and a surplus of 2.8 per cent of GDP in the target year 2029-30 (around £100 billion). For PSNFL, there is a 60 per cent chance of it lying between 78 per cent of GDP and 90 per cent of GDP in 2029-30. This reflects the uncertainty inherent in any medium-term fiscal forecast given the multiple economic factors that can affect the public finances and the scale of the shocks that can hit the economy over such a period. This is illustrated by the frequency with which large adverse shocks have hit the economy over the last two decades, as outlined earlier in the chapter. These types of downside risks mean that the probability distribution is weighted towards higher levels of borrowing and debt. While risks are skewed to the downside, outcomes above and below the median forecast remain broadly equally likely, based on current stated Government policy.

Change in the margins against fiscal targets

7.20 Chart 7.6 decomposes the change in margins for the current budget and PSNFL targets in the central forecast compared to last November. The current budget has a reduced margin of £7 billion, while PSNFL is unchanged:

  • Underlying pre-measures forecast changes between the Budget 2025 forecast and the March 2026 forecast increased the margin by £8 billion for both the current budget and the net liabilities target.[footnote 87] This was largely driven by upward revisions in March to the receipts forecast due to higher forecast equity prices, and a lower debt interest spending forecast as a result of lower gilt rates and RPI inflation at that time.

  • The effects of policy measures announced between Budget 2025 and the March 2026 forecast lowered the current budget and PSNFL margins by £6 billion.

  • Underlying pre-measures forecast changes since the March forecast have reduced the current budget margin by £11 billion and the PSNFL margin by £5 billion.3 This largely reflects higher debt interest spending, mainly as a result of increased borrowing costs and inflation, and higher welfare spending due to inflation, described further in Chapter 6. The impact of pre-measures forecast changes on PSNFL is lower because of a higher forecast for nominal GDP growth in 2029-30, which lowers PSNFL as a share of GDP.[footnote 88]

Margins against successive fiscal mandates

7.21 The margin against the Government’s fiscal mandate of £15 billion is around half of the average margin that previous Chancellors have left against their fiscal mandate since 2010. Chart 7.7 shows that at 56 per cent, the probability of meeting the target is judged to be broadly in line with the mean and median since the pandemic. The £15 billion margin is only slightly lower than the average revision to pre-measures borrowing in the third year of the forecast since the pandemic, which is £18 billion.[footnote 89] It is under half of the median three-year-ahead difference between forecast and outturn, which is £34 billion.[footnote 90]

7.22 The margins shown in Chart 7.7 have often been against rules that targeted the fourth or fifth year of the forecast period. At this forecast, the current Government’s fiscal mandate is now assessed at the third year of the forecast. The Charter also requires the Government to set detailed spending plans for three years ahead at spending reviews every two years. This means that, from the next spending review, the Government will be required to have detailed spending allocations for the year in which the fiscal targets bind. Welfare cap

7.24 The welfare cap is a limit for government spending on certain social security benefits and tax credits in the final year of a given Parliament. Since its introduction in 2014, the welfare cap has been revised upwards frequently to account for inflation and changes in welfare demand. The Charter states that the OBR will make a formal assessment of spending against the welfare cap and margin at the first Budget of each new Parliament, and will monitor welfare spending against the pathway and margin at each Budget before the formal assessment.

7.25 The Government set a welfare cap of £194.5 billion in 2029-30 at the October 2024 forecast, and a margin for the cap that rises each year to reach 5 per cent in 2029-30. Spending against the welfare cap in 2029-30 has risen by £5 billion since the November 2025 forecast, largely due to higher in-work and health-related universal credit caseloads, along with higher spending forecasts for supported housing. This results in the welfare cap being on course not to be met by £3 billion once the margin is included.

Balance sheet and fiscal affordability metrics

7.26 The assessment of the Government’s performance against its medium-term fiscal targets provides limited information on the overall sustainability of the fiscal position. In recognition of this, the Charter sets out that the “OBR will consider a wide range of factors and dimensions relating to the sustainability of the public finances”. In this chapter, we have included analysis of the UK’s overall fiscal position compared to the past, provided comparisons of key fiscal indicators in the UK compared to other advanced economies, and summarised some of the key conclusions from our most recent analysis of long-term fiscal sustainability in the 2026 FRS. This section provides a summary assessment of a range of balance sheet, debt affordability and debt stabilisation metrics, which can also be used as indicators of fiscal sustainability.

7.27 Table 7.3 presents this dashboard of metrics that shows: first (top two panels), their levels and how these compare with the medians from 1967-68 to 2006-07 (the four decades preceding the financial crisis) and from 2007-08 to 2018-19; and second (lowest panel), whether they are improving or deteriorating in each year of the forecast. It shows that:

  • Balance sheet stock measures all remain in a significantly worse position than both the pre-2007 and the 2007-2019 medians across the forecast period.

  • The financing and cost of debt measures are also generally in a worse position than the pre-crisis median. The central government net cash requirement remains above the pre-2007 median for the majority of the forecast period. Net interest costs are also above the pre-2007 median as a share of GDP across the forecast period, and close to the pre-2007 median as a share of revenue.

  • The primary balance (non-interest revenue minus non-interest spending) is expected to be in a better position than the pre-financial crisis median from 2028-29 onwards. It is forecast to improve from a 1.5 per cent of GDP deficit (£47 billion) in 2025-26 to a 1.7 per cent of GDP (£65 billion) surplus in 2031-32.

  • However, the debt-stabilising primary balance, which is the level of the primary balance at which debt remains constant as a share of GDP, is forecast to be a surplus which rises across the forecast period. By contrast, in both the pre-financial crisis period and the 2007-2019 period, governments could run deficits of 0.4 per cent of GDP and 1.5 per cent of GDP respectively, and still stabilise debt.

  • The difference between the primary balance and the debt-stabilising primary balance gives the debt stabilisation gap. This gap is positive until 2028-29, which means that debt is forecast to rise up to this year, but becomes negative from 2029-30 onwards due to the forecast improvement in the primary balance, which means that debt is forecast to be marginally falling in this period. The long-term trends and outlook for the debt-stabilising primary balance are discussed further in Box 7.1.

Box 7.1: Long-term trends in the growth-corrected interest rate, “R-G”

A key indicator of fiscal sustainability is the growth-corrected interest rate, often referred to as ‘R-G’, which is the difference between the cost of servicing debt and the growth rate of the economy.a If the effective nominal interest rate (R) exceeds nominal GDP growth (G), so R-G is positive, then a primary surplus is required to stabilise debt as a share of GDP, all else equal. Conversely, when G exceeds R, and so R-G is negative, governments can, in principle, run a primary deficit without debt as a share of GDP rising. Together with the level of the debt stock and financial transactions, R-G determines the debt-stabilising primary balance.b When debt levels are high, a given positive level of R-G implies a larger debt-stabilising primary balance.

Chart A shows trends in R-G and the debt-stabilising primary balance since the Second World War. Up to the end of the 1970s, growth was consistently higher than the effective interest rate on government debt, and so R-G was negative, which meant that the debt-stabilising primary balance was very low at, on average, -5 per cent. This facilitated the rapid reduction in debt as a share of GDP seen over this period. The 1980s saw nominal growth rates fall below nominal interest rates, and so R-G turned positive. It remained positive for most years up to the financial crisis in 2008, with an average value of 1 per cent over the period. However, a low stock of debt meant the debt-stabilising primary balance averaged close to zero per cent of GDP.

Following the global financial crisis (GFC), the effective interest rate fell to an average of 3 per cent between 2009-10 and 2018-19, the lowest rate since the 1950s. While growth was also weak over much of this period, these very low interest rates meant that R-G turned negative, reaching -1.3 per cent in 2018-19. Despite this, debt levels rose, largely because the primary deficit averaged 2.1 per cent of GDP higher than the level required to keep debt stable.

Since 2022, interest rates have risen sharply and economic growth has remained subdued. As a result, R-G has increased from -3.5 per cent in 2022-23 to -1.1 per cent in 2025-26. Market interest rates are currently higher than the effective interest rate on the stock of debt, so as the debt stock is refinanced over time the effective interest rate will rise towards the market rate. This contributes to the forecast increase in R-G from -0.2 per cent in 2027-28 to 0.4 per cent in 2031-32.

This would be a return to the generally positive levels of R-G seen in the three decades leading up to the financial crisis, even though market interest rates are currently around 1.7 per cent lower than the post-war average. However, the level of debt is now much higher than in the pre-financial crisis period which, along with an increased use of financial transactions, increases the debt-stabilising primary balance for a given level of R-G. The debt-stabilising primary balance is expected to rise from 0.4 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 1.5 per cent by 2031-32, 3 percentage points higher than the 2007-2019 median (Table 7.3).

Risk and uncertainty

7.28 All economic and fiscal forecasts are inherently subject to significant risk and uncertainty. It is inevitable that unforeseen events will drive economic and fiscal outcomes away from any central forecast. In recent years, large negative shocks, consistently weak GDP growth and significant policy changes have generated substantial revisions to forecasts from one fiscal event to the next. We use a range of tools to highlight this uncertainty and to meet the requirement in the Charter that we provide analysis of the risks surrounding the fiscal outlook. These include:

  • detailing specific risks to our economic and fiscal forecasts, focusing on those which appear most material at the time;

  • fan charts that reflect the chances of shocks of different sizes – through stochastic simulations and past central forecast deviations from outturns – to illustrate the uncertainty around key economic and fiscal variables, including, as set out in paragraphs 7.18 and 7.19, the fiscal aggregates targeted in the Government’s fiscal rules;

  • sensitivity analysis that shows the responsiveness of the path of the current budget deficit to changes in key forecast variables, including gilt yields and nominal GDP growth; and

  • scenarios that illustrate the potential channels through which changes in energy prices could affect the public finances.

Specific risks

7.29 The most important specific sources of risk to the economy forecast include:

  • The evolution of the Middle East conflict, and its implications for interest rates and inflation, which has sharply pushed up energy prices this year and led to disruption to wider international trade flows. Energy markets remain volatile – at the time of finalising this report, oil and gas futures pricing was close to the top of the range observed since the beginning of the Middle East conflict. From paragraph 7.33 onwards, we explain the results of a detailed set of scenarios that illustrate the potential economic and fiscal implications of alternative paths for energy prices. This highlights that the fiscal impact is particularly dependent on changes in financial conditions and the extent of the pass-through of an inflation shock to wages, which would serve to boost nominal tax bases. This is particularly important given that personal tax thresholds are currently frozen. In addition, any inflationary shock would create further pressure on departmental spending by eroding real-terms Spending Review settlements.

  • The outlook for productivity growth, a key driver of the economic and fiscal forecasts, is highly uncertain. The development and adoption of artificial intelligence could have a significant positive effect – our central forecast is for it to boost productivity growth by 0.2 percentage points a year by the medium term – but the scale and timing of any effect is highly uncertain. An additional uncertainty relates to challenges in accurately measuring historical productivity. As discussed in Box 2.2, ONS revisions to historical average hours suggest that UK productivity growth slowed after the financial crisis, but that the magnitude of the slowdown was closer to international comparators than previously suggested. This was driven by average hours growth being materially lower than previously estimated. Any change to the outlook for productivity could have a significant impact on the public finances. In the November 2025 EFO, we illustrated that if annual productivity growth were 0.5 percentage points higher or lower in the medium term than our central forecast, borrowing would be around £50 billion lower or £40 billion higher by 2030-31.

  • The outlook for the labour market, including from the effects of an ageing population and from migration, provides several sources of uncertainty. We assume that the ageing population will have a moderate adverse impact on average hours worked and labour market participation. However, the forecast for average hours worked is particularly uncertain due to recent historical revisions, as outlined above. There are also significant risks around the size and composition of future migration flows, given the post-Brexit change in migration regime and the recent spike and subsequent fall in net migration. In addition, there are risks around the outlook for unemployment. In the March 2026 EFO, we produced scenarios on the fiscal implications of alternative paths for the labour market. These suggested that if unemployment returned to its estimated equilibrium rate two years earlier than the central forecast, borrowing could be £16 billion a year lower on average, or if it instead peaked at a higher 6.8 per cent, borrowing could be an average of £20 billion a year higher than our central forecast.

7.30 There are also an additional set of specific fiscal and policy-related risks:

  • The cost of servicing government debt – which had already increased sharply since 2021 before rising further following the onset of the conflict in Iran. As explained in Chapter 2, UK government borrowing costs have been volatile recently with the 10-year yield ranging from around 4.5 to 5.5 per cent since March. But yields within this range are not unusual by historical standards. As a result of the recent rise in yields, debt interest spending is now forecast to rise to 4.2 per cent of GDP (£160 billion) in 2031-32, compared to 1.7 per cent of GDP (£39 billion) in 2019-20. Paragraph 7.32 sets out that a 1 percentage point change in gilt yields and Bank Rate expectations across the forecast in either direction could lead to an increase or decrease of £16 billion in the current budget deficit in the medium term.

  • There continue to be a wide range of pressures on departmental spending. These include higher inflation since March, which reduces real-terms departmental spending within fixed nominal spending limits, and the risk of higher-than-expected pay settlements. Beyond the current spending review, after accounting for spending commitments in areas including the NHS, defence and schools, the total spending assumptions currently set by the Government for the likely next spending review period imply ‘unprotected’ areas of day-to-day spending could face a 2.6 per cent a year real-terms reduction in the final three years of the forecast. Spending would have to be £11 billion higher in 2031-32 for ‘unprotected’ spending not to fall in real terms from 2028-29. The Government has set out a longer-term ambition to reform social care, which the Health Foundation previously estimated could cost between £3.5 billion and £17 billion a year.[footnote 91] The commitment to increase defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035 would cost around £35 billion in 2026-27 terms.

  • There is significant uncertainty around the outlook for welfare spending, especially on disability- and health-related benefits, where caseloads have increased sharply since the pandemic. We continue to assume that the caseloads will rise in the forecast, but at a slower rate than that seen to date. If caseloads were to continue to grow at their post-pandemic rate, spending in 2031-32 would be roughly £25 billion higher than in our central forecast in 2031-32, but if pre-pandemic rates were restored, then spending could be around £13 billion lower in 2031-32.

  • The forecast rise in the tax-to-GDP ratio accounts for around three-fifths of the current planned medium-term consolidation of the public finances. However, there are several risks around this forecast. Much of the increase is from rising income tax and national insurance contributions which is highly sensitive to growth in nominal earnings, especially with personal tax thresholds frozen until 2030-31. Capital taxes also account for a significant portion of the forecast rise, but they are highly dependent on future equity prices and are sensitive to behavioural responses from affected taxpayers who are more typically a more mobile part of the tax base. Further, the forecast assumes that the indexation of fuel duty and reversal of the 5p cut will be implemented in July 2027. The forecast also assumes the tax gap – a measure of tax compliance – will decline over the forecast period following the recent period where it has remained broadly flat after rising in the 2010s. More broadly, a higher level of tax take increases the risk that incentives within the tax system distort or constrain economic activity by more or less than expected.

7.31 Some steps have been taken to address previously identified fiscal risks. As discussed in more detail in Chapter 3, the Government has announced it will replace the state pension triple lock with an adjusted triple lock from April 2030 which should significantly reduce the projected increase in the cost of the state pension over the long term. Additionally, as set out above, the fiscal mandate now targets the third year of the forecast. This means that, from the next spending review, the Government will be required to have detailed spending allocations for the year in which the fiscal targets bind which should reduce the risks around meeting these targets.

Sensitivities

7.32 Sensitivity analysis estimates how unit changes to key forecast variables would, in isolation, affect the current budget deficit relative to our central forecast.[footnote 92] Chart 7.9 shows that:

  • A 0.1 percentage point reduction in nominal GDP growth from 2027-28 is estimated to increase the current budget deficit by £5 billion in 2029-30 and £9 billion in 2031-32.

  • A 1 percentage point reduction in the effective tax rate from 2027-28 is expected to increase the current budget deficit by £35 billion in 2029-30 and £38 billion in 2031-32, assuming no wider macroeconomic impacts.

  • A 1 percentage point increase in gilt yields on new debt issued and on Bank Rate expectations across the forecast period, directly via its effect on debt interest payments, is expected to increase the current budget deficit by £13 billion in 2029-30 and £16 billion in 2031-32.

  • A 1 percentage point rise in RPI and CPIH inflation in each year of the forecast period, via its effect on accrued interest on index-linked gilts alone, is expected to increase the current budget deficit by £9 billion in 2029-30 and £11 billion in 2031-32.[footnote 93]

Scenarios

7.33 Energy prices have been volatile recently and their future evolution will be important to the economic and fiscal outlook, with significant implications for inflation, interest rates and GDP growth. To explore these factors, we present two alternative scenarios for energy prices, shown in Chart 7.10. The energy price paths are calibrated using an option-implied distribution of market pricing, taking one standard deviation above or below the central path implied by futures in the near term:

  • In our severe shock scenario, oil prices peak at around $115 a barrel in the first half of 2027 and the shock is more persistent than the market pricing in our central forecast, with prices remaining at or above $100 a barrel throughout 2027 and staying elevated until 2031. Gas prices reach a peak of 275 pence a therm, with prices remaining over 150 pence a therm throughout 2027 before gradually returning to the central forecast path. In both cases, the peak is near the highs observed following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

  • In our orderly recovery scenario, oil and gas prices fall back more quickly than assumed in our central forecast, and converge on our March 2026 forecast path in the medium term. Oil prices reach a trough of around $55 a barrel in the second quarter of 2027 and gas prices a trough of around 55 pence a therm during the third quarter, and both return to their March 2026 forecast path in 2029.

7.34 We take a layered approach to illustrate the potential channels through which these alternative paths may affect the economic and fiscal outlook, rather than providing a single estimate of the possible impact. In both scenarios, we first set out the potential direct impact on the economy and public finances, and then layer on the potential implications for interest rates and gilt yields. In the severe shock scenario, we set out further potential implications arising from second-round effects in inflation and increased pressures on departmental spending plans arising from higher inflation. The scenarios were informed by the Oxford Economics Global Economic Model, alongside our own judgement.

Severe shock

7.35 We set out four channels of potential impacts on the economy and public finances in the severe shock scenario (for which the key economic implications are shown in Chart 7.11):

  • The pure energy shock leads to a peak in CPI inflation of around 6 per cent next year – about 2¼ percentage points above our central forecast – and a reduction in GDP growth in 2027 to below ½ a per cent – ¾ of a percentage point below our central forecast. In 2031, the level of real GDP is ¼ per cent lower than in our central forecast, though the level of nominal GDP is slightly higher. RHDI per person is persistently lower than our central forecast, and only recovers to its pre-pandemic level after a decade, in 2029-30. By assumption, there is no adjustment in interest rates.

  • We then illustrate a potential tightening in financial conditions resulting from the shock. Relative to our central forecast, we assume an additional upward adjustment to Bank Rate of around 1 percentage point by the second half of 2027, and a persistent increase in gilt yields of around 1 percentage point.[footnote 94] This leads to a further reduction in real GDP growth in 2027.

  • Possible second-round effects increase nominal earnings growth by an average of ½ of a percentage point each year from 2027 to 2029, and CPI inflation by an average ¼ of a percentage point. This results in a further upward adjustment in Bank Rate and gilt yields and increases the size of the nominal economy and key tax bases. But it has little impact on the path of real GDP growth or RHDI per person. Both whether second-round effects emerge and their potential scale are highly uncertain.

  • We also illustrate the implied erosion in real departmental spending power due to the higher inflation. This is the additional spending that would be required to maintain the same real-terms value of departmental spending as in our central forecast. Any adjustment would not happen automatically as departmental spending limits are set in nominal terms and are a discretionary policy choice for the Government.

Chart 7.11: Severe shock scenario CPI inflation and real GDP growth

Source: ONS, OBR

7.36 Chart 7.12 shows the potential implications for borrowing from each of these different channels in the severe shock scenario relative to our central forecast:

  • The pure energy shock is estimated to add £7 billion to borrowing in 2027-28, as increased spending on index-linked gilts more than offsets higher oil and gas revenues. It adds £4 billion in 2031-32 as higher welfare spending more than offsets a small increase in receipts arising from a larger nominal economy.[footnote 95]

  • Tightening financial conditions could add a further £11 billion, on average, to borrowing over the forecast, due to higher debt interest costs.

  • Second-round effects could reduce borrowing by increasing amounts, reaching £13 billion in 2031-32, as domestically generated inflation from wages pushes up receipts by more than spending, particularly due to frozen personal tax thresholds.

  • Taken together, all these factors could increase borrowing by around £6 billion in 2031-32 relative to the central forecast. The pressures on the public finances would be compounded by a £13 billion erosion in real-terms departmental spending power.[footnote 96]

Orderly recovery

7.37 We set out two channels of impact for the economy and public finances in the orderly recovery scenario.[footnote 97] The implications for CPI inflation and real GDP growth are shown in Chart 7.13:

  • The pure energy price fall results in more rapid disinflation than in our central forecast, with CPI inflation falling to 2¼ per cent in 2027 (1¼ percentage points lower than the central forecast). There is higher real GDP growth of 1½ per cent in 2027 (½ of a percentage point above our central forecast) while the lower inflation largely reverses the near-term decline in RHDI per person seen in our central forecast. By 2031, the level of real GDP is ¼ of a per cent higher than in our central forecast, while the level of nominal GDP is similar. As in the severe shock scenario, there is no adjustment in interest rates by assumption.

  • We assume that there is financial easing as the energy shock subsides, such that Bank Rate remains flat in 2027 before it largely converges with our central forecast by mid-2028.[footnote 98] Gilt yields are lower across the forecast period, as we assume there is around ½ of a percentage point reduction in the risk premium, taking gilt yields around halfway back to the March EFO forecast levels. This has only modest implications for real GDP growth.

Source: ONS, OBR

7.38 Chart 7.14 shows the implications for PSNB of the orderly recovery scenario relative to our central forecast. These are modest compared to the severe shock scenario, as the near-term change in energy prices is smaller. The fiscal implications of the pure fall in energy prices largely track inflation. Lower inflation reduces debt interest spending on index-linked gilts in 2027-28, but then debt interest spending is marginally higher in the two subsequent years because inflation is slightly higher than in the central forecast. By 2031-32, borrowing is broadly unchanged, as lower welfare spending due to lower inflation offsets lower receipts from a smaller nominal economy. Financial easing further reduces borrowing by £5 billion on average over the forecast period, due to the lower path for Bank Rate and gilt yields.
